News.title: Queues at EU airports expected to worsen ahead of new rule starting in September
News.content:
Queues at EU airports expected to worsen ahead of new rule starting in September

EU member states are allowed to pause EES checks when queues become too long, but this rule will change in September and delays could be experienced as a result

View 3 Images Passengers wait in long queues at passport control in the departures terminal of Brussels Airport in Brussels, Belgium, on June 29, 2026 (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Wait times at European borders could worsen as a new rule is rolled out in September.

‌



Borders across the EU have experienced long queues since April when new Entry/Exit System (EES) was fully rolled out. The ESS applies to all Brits entering Europe.

‌



Travellers must register upon their first entry to a Schengen country. This requires their photographs and fingerprints to be taken.

‌



This process has been caused long delays at border control across European airports, with some travellers waiting hours and others missing their flights.

View 3 Images Travellers must register upon their first entry to a Schengen country (Image: Getty)

From September 6, a flexibility allowance introduced across Europe is due to expire.

‌



Presently, EU member states are allowed to pause EES checks in "exceptional circumstances". This includes when queues become too long.

The EU border security agency Frontex has said that the flexibility will not be renewed in September, despite calls from industry bodies to allow the renewal.

Countries could again see long queues at airports when flexibility expires.

‌



At some airports, the machines are required to be restarted when they become overwhelmed.

Air France-KLM told Politico : "When lines form during the busy summer months, the system is shut off to ensure smooth transit at our hubs in Paris and Amsterdam."

Other hubs, such as Brussels Airport, that have reported problems with the technology where the system is still not fully operational.

‌



Other issues with the new system have emerged including taking the fingerprints of the elderly.

Last month, the head of Ryanair has criticised the EU's rules.

View 3 Images Ryanair has told passengers it will not wait for them (Image: Placebo365/Getty)

‌



Speaking on The Travel Expert podcast, however, Michael O'Leary said it was still down to passengers to leave enough time to get to their boarding gate, or risk being left behind.

"We will not wait for anybody," he said.

"Our priority is to those passengers who are at the boarding gate when boarding starts.

Article continues below

"If you're not at the boarding gate when we finish boarding, the plane is going without you."

Hundreds of travellers on a range of airlines have missed planes since April, including Ryanair who watched their flights take off without them because of extreme delays at passport control.

News.title: Dad and son gouge eyes of mourners as funeral wake turns into 'bar room brawl'
News.content:
Dad and son gouge eyes of mourners as funeral wake turns into 'bar room brawl'

A judge told all three in the courtroom that 'this was an entirely disgraceful event... all three of you should be ashamed of yourselves' as he passed down his sentencing

View 4 Images Liam Redmond jnr outside Liverpool Crown Court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

A father and his two sons left a lorry driver with a severe facial injury requiring nine stitches when a funeral "descended into something akin to a bar room brawl".

‌



The man has been left with permanent scarring after nine stitches were required to his face after the family went postal at a wake, with the three men hurling pint glasses and gouging at the eyes of mourners following the funeral service.

‌



Given the father had previously become violent at another memorial gathering just three years prior, a judge has scolded the family for the brawl in a public courtroom: "This was an entirely disgraceful event. All three of you should be ashamed of yourselves."

‌



Liverpool Crown Court heard on Thursday that the Redmonds, all of Holm Lane in Prenton, Wirral, were in attendance of a wake held at the Prenton Golf Club on the afternoon of 17 October 2024 following a funeral.

Their connection to the deceased remains unclear, but the father and sons are understood to have been unfamiliar to witnesses of the incident in question. It is understood that witnesses, however, "thought that the defendants were inappropriately dressed" for the event in question.

View 4 Images Luke Redmond outside Liverpool Crown Court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

‌



Prosecutor Henry Riding told the court that the wake had been scheduled to finish at 7pm, with golf course manager Kate Verdin-Walsh announcing last orders shortly before 6.45pm. She described the atmosphere as "good" with the service "passing without any untoward incident" until last drinks were called and staff members then "alerted her to shouting in the bar area".

At the scene, Ms Verdin-Walsh discovered "12 to 15 persons in a circle, appearing to act as a buffer between two males who were arguing and shouting". According to the Liverpool Echo, Liam Redmond snr was reportedly amongst those involved, and was observed shouting at another man as the latter "tried to back away".

Having "managed to calm him down", the now 61-year-old and his sons — who had previously been described as "squaring up and showboating" — were then escorted from the premises by staff. However, the father then dragged another man to the ground near to the exit. It was then "large scale fight broke out", the court heard.

‌



The brawl was apparently triggered by a man grabbing at Redmond snr's daughter as she attempted to follow him and her brothers out of the venue. The man who had been floored "put his arm around her back to keep her in the room", and was apparently unaware of her connection to those who had been removed.

What followed was a "lot of pushing and fighting", leading to one of the sons allegedly hurling a pint glass into the crowd. The glass struck Ms Verdin-Walsh on the head, causing a small lump and resulting in her needing hospital treatment.

Witness Ronald Hancox subsequently stated that he had observed Redmond snr "pressing his thumb inside the eye of another male", prompting him to intervene by striking the defendant. Another attendee, Carl Hancox, also witnessed the father "striking a male called Billy" before forcing his thumbs into the victim's eyes.

‌



When he also rushed to assist this victim, he remembered that "all three defendants turned their attentions on him", resulting in him being punched and kicked to the head while on the ground. Roberts snr was then said to have similarly "shoved his thumbs into his eye, like he had done to Billy".

View 4 Images Liam Redmond jnr outside Liverpool Crown Court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

William Donaldson, the uncle of the man who was first dragged to the ground during the incident, told police he had "run into the centre of the fight to try protect his nephew". Prosecutor Mr Riding said: "He saw a glass being thrown by one of the males but ended up on the floor, being struck multiple times by the younger of the two males, who attempted to gouge out his eyes with his fingers."

‌



Mr Donaldson suffered a "split" nose in the attack, which he believed was caused by a glass bottle. He attended hospital the following day, where the wound was closed with a total of nine stitches.

The HGV driver was also forced to take a fortnight off work after being left with fragments of glass in his eye. In a victim impact statement read to the court, he said of the scar on his face: "I don't really go out much any more so that I don't have to explain it to people. I no longer pop down to the pub. I get nervous about strange places and people. I was always easy going and could chat to anyone. I always enjoyed a laugh and socialising, but not any more."

Liam Redmond snr has 16 previous convictions for 24 offences dating back to 1978, including a nine-month sentence for attempted wounding in 1990. In May 2022, he was handed a 12-month community order for affray relating to a "fight caused by the defendant at a wake in a hotel in 2021".

‌



Defence barrister Lloyd Morgan told the court his client suffered from emphysema, adding: "Mr Roberts snr receives Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment. He receives about £900 per month. He has various outgoings. The report does recommend a rehabilitation activity requirement and an alcohol abstinence monitoring requirement."

Neither Liam Redmond jnr, 25, nor Luke Redmond, 23, had any previous convictions. Representing Liam Redmond jnr, Nick Cockrell told the court: "This was, in this defendant's life, an isolated incident, almost two years ago now, admittedly one committed when he was in drink. He does still drink from time to time, as any young person does. He is a self employed plasterer."

Luke Redmond's barrister Cheryl Mottram said her client had not reoffended since the incident and was "very remorseful". All three defendants admitted affray on the day they had been due to stand trial.

‌



View 4 Images Liam Redmond snr outside Liverpool Crown Court (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Liam Redmond snr, who appeared in the dock wearing a navy blue cardigan over a light blue shirt and tie, was sentenced to nine months in prison, suspended for 18 months. He was also ordered to complete up to 10 days of rehabilitation activity and a 90-day alcohol abstinence monitoring requirement. Liam Redmond jnr, wearing a light blue shirt and tie, and Luke Redmond, dressed in a grey suit and glasses, were each given 12-month community orders with 15 days of rehabilitation activity and 80 hours of unpaid work.

All three men were also ordered to pay Mr Donaldson £250 each in compensation. Sentencing them, Judge Garrett Byrne said: "On that date, you were all in attendance at a wake at Prenton Golf Club. You, along with everybody, it seems to me, were under the influence of alcohol. There appears to have been some words said, and a fight broke out.

‌



"This was, on any view, an entirely disgraceful event. All three of you should be ashamed of yourselves. What was supposed to be a solemn and respectful event descended into something akin to a bar room brawl.

"It started when you, Mr Redmond snr, dragged the nephew down. Mr Donaldson ran over to help his nephew, and the fight started. Glasses were thrown, various injuries were suffered by a number of different people, including the manager, including Carl Hancox, but, perhaps most seriously of all, William Donaldson, who suffered a very serious injury to his nose.

"He had nine stitches to close that unpleasant wound. He was left with a permanent scar. He was left with glass fragments in his eyes. Although it is not entirely clear which of you caused the injuries to Mr Donaldson, it is clear that you were all active participants in the fight."

Article continues below

Judge Byrne told Redmond snr his previous conviction "bore a striking similarity" to the latest offence, adding: "It was another wake. You were also intoxicated.

"I accept that you have not reoffended. None of you have reoffended since this offence. You have shown genuine remorse. I accept that you have medical conditions. You showed good compliance on your community order, albeit it did not stop you committing this offence."

News.title: UK construction company enters liquidation with over £430k debts
News.content:
UK construction company enters liquidation with over £430k debts

The UK 'nationally recognised leader in construction services' has been appointed liquidators as files show the company has outstanding debts

View 2 Images The construction company has entered liquidation with debts (Image: Getty)

A UK construction company has been appointed liquidators with over £430k in debts.

‌



The Ilford based company GTG Civils Ltd was appointed the liquidators on August 3, 2026 after just six years in business.

‌



According to Companies House, the building firm was incorporated on July 9, 2020.

‌



View 2 Images Documents on Companies House display over £400k in debts (Image: Getty )

The nature of the business is listed as construction of domestic buildings and its website claims it is 'a nationally recognised leader in construction services'.

The company has 'a large pool of experienced labourers based in London and all over the UK' to provide work across the country.

‌



The website states: "Our team of experienced and highly skilled contractors specializes in groundworks, providing expert solutions tailored to a wide range of projects, from industrial complexes to large commercial developments."

They carry out commercial projects and well as residential builds.

The firm's latest public accounts dated up to July 31, 2025 show £430,007 in amounts falling due within one year. The Gazette notes Grace Jones and David Perkins both of Parker Andrews Limited as liquidators.

‌



The collapse of GTG comes amid difficulties for several construction companies, with many plummeting into liquidation this year.

On July 6 a British construction firm specialising in affordable housing collapsed into administration after seven years in business.

Oxfordshire-based Agile Property and Homes designed and built low-carbon modular homes for those in housing need before its closure.

Article continues below

In June, Juma Construction Group also fell into liquidation with over 40 years of experience in the industry, according to the firm's website.

News.title: UK trains cancelled: Avanti and Northern Rail services hit by power outage
News.content:
Avanti West Coast services are affected by the disruption

National Rail warned of 'major rail disruption' in the Greater Manchester area and the north-west of England, with trains cancelled, rescheduled or delayed by up to two hours

UK trains cancelled: Avanti and Northern Rail services hit by power outage

There is "major rail disruption" in the Greater Manchester area and the north-west of England, National Rail has warned.

An electrical failure at Network Rail's Manchester Rail Operating Centre has led to trains being cancelled, rescheduled or delayed since Thursday afternoon.

Services operated by Avanti West Coast, CrossCountry, East Midlands Railway, London Northwestern Railway, Northern, TransPennine Express and Transport for Wales are affected.

The disruption is expected to last until the end of Thursday, National Rail added.

News.title: Theme park to close 'legendary' ride with 'world’s tallest vertical loop' forever - after three decades of thrills
News.content:
Theme park to close 'legendary' ride with 'world’s tallest vertical loop' forever - after three decades of thrills

A Florida based theme park has shut a 'legendary' once record-breaking ride after three decades as part of a $100 million investment scheme to revamp the destination

View 3 Images The once record-breaking roller coaster has closed

An iconic theme park ride has closed forever after thrilling visitors for three decades.

‌



Kumba, a once record-breaking roller coaster in Florida stopped taking passengers on board on August 2.

‌



The Busch Gardens Tampa Bay ride first opened as a side attraction to the then-new Busch Brewery location.

‌



View 3 Images Kumba, a once-record-holding roller coaster at Busch Gardens Tampa Bay, is set to close on August 2

At the time of opening in 1993 Kumba featured the world’s tallest vertical loop at 114 feet. It was also the tallest, fastest, and longest roller coaster in Florida.

These records have since been broken.

‌



The ride also had a 135-foot drop, a dive loop, a zero-g roll, a cobra roll, and a pair of interlocking corkscrews and put the theme park on the map for thrill seekers, competing with Disney and Universal.

The ride was met by fans immediately, but became less of a draw to the park as more advanced roller coasters were built.

Earlier this year Busch announced that the roller coaster would be closing shortly after its 33rd birthday.

‌



View 3 Images Guests can expect a new ride to be built in its place

Busch Gardens paid tribute to the ride on social media, writing: “Debuting in 1993, Kumba set a new standard for thrill rides! It was Florida’s tallest, fastest, and longest roller coaster when it opened, and it featured the world’s tallest vertical loop.

"From its 7 exhilarating inversions to its iconic roar sound, Kumba has left its mark on Busch Gardens and will be remembered as an icon of the park.”

‌



The statement added that a sequel roller coaster is set to open following the ride's closure.

The statement continued: “As part of our evolution and commitment to delivering innovative attractions, we are happy to announce Kumba’s Revenge! This new attraction is a part of our $100 million investment that will elevate Busch Gardens as Florida’s thrill leader and enhance our guest experience.

"Kumba’s Revenge is an extension of an already legendary coaster, and it will allow its spirit to live on as we enter a new era of thrills.”

Article continues below

Further details about the new attraction are yet to be revealed.

News.title: UK heatwave impacts high street shopping as retail footfall declines in July
News.content:
UK heatwave impacts high street shopping as retail footfall declines in July

Total UK retail footfall was down 2.1% on a year earlier in July, but an improvement on the 3.4% drop seen in June amid heatwave conditions, according to British Retail Consortium (BRC)-Sensormatic data

View 2 Images So many people shop online these days! (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Heatwave conditions continued to weigh heavily on shopper footfall in July, with the high street particularly badly hit, figures suggest.

‌



Total UK footfall dropped 2.1% compared with a year earlier, though this marked an improvement on June's 3.4% decline, according to British Retail Consortium (BRC)-Sensormatic data.

‌



High street footfall fell 3.8% year-on-year in July, up from June's 6.2% plunge. Shopping centre footfall was also down, by 1.4% year-on-year, although this represented an improvement on June's 2.5% drop.

‌



View 2 Images There are ongoing challenges facing larger urban centres during spells of extreme heat, Sensormatic said. (Image: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock)

Woman misdiagnosed with aggressive cancer had hysterectomy after lab mix-up READ MORE :

England recorded the weakest performance of any UK nation with an overall footfall decline of 3%, with London down 5.3%, highlighting the ongoing challenges facing larger urban centres during spells of extreme heat, Sensormatic said.

BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said: "The heatwave continued to bear down on retail footfall in July, with high streets worst affected. London was hit particularly hard as soaring temperatures made tube and train travel less attractive, with some commuters and shoppers opting to stay home.

‌



"Nonetheless, it was still an improvement on the previous month's figures, when record-breaking sunshine saw footfall fall by an even bigger margin."

She said: "Climate change continues to deliver more and more extreme temperatures in the UK.

"Retailers are responding by investing in both mitigations – such as more air conditioning and more efficient refrigeration units – and in sustainability initiatives aimed at reducing carbon emissions.

Article continues below

"Unfortunately, business rates often punish stores for such investments, showing the need for government to look again at this broken system."

Andy Sumpter, from Sensormatic, revealed that six of the first seven months of this year fared worse than the corresponding period last year. He said: "The exceptionally hot and historically dry weather is likely to have been a significant factor, discouraging shopping trips and particularly impacting high streets.

"While the UK has yet another new prime minister, retail is yet to experience any meaningful 'Burnham bounce'. For retailers, the focus remains on converting these more selective visits into meaningful spend as the summer progresses."

News.title: Man arrested over wildfire says 'this is going to destroy my life' as body found
News.content:
Man arrested over wildfire says 'this is going to destroy my life' as body found

A 65-year-old man was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the fire - he is suspected of "recklessly causing" the blaze on Monday that is believed to have been sparked by a chain saw

View 3 Images A wildfire in Calaveras County, California (Image: Getty)

A burned body has been found inside a home after a wildfire scorched parts of central California, with the authorities believing a chainsaw started the fatal blaze.

‌



Authorities said on Thursday, August 6, that the fire is believed to have been started by sparks from a chainsaw - one man has been arrested in connection to the blaze.

‌



65-year-old Herbert Wayne Smith was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the fire. Herbert Wayne Smith is suspected of "recklessly causing" the blaze on Monday.

‌



View 3 Images Firefighter fights blaze in California (Image: Getty)

Mr Smith told KCRA-TV that he was using a chain saw to cut some scrap wood when it ignited.

"I'm so sorry for everything that's happened," he said.

‌



"This is going to destroy my life, one way or another."

The wildfire has destroyed seven structures and scorched more than 15 square miles (39 square km) of forest in the Sierra Nevada foothills of Calaveras County.

It is believed that the fire was cause while "operating equipment capable of producing sparks" without clearing flammable vegetation as required, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Wildfire scorched an area in California (Image: Getty)

Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges.

Investigators will determine whether the fire contributed to the death of the person found in a burned home in the area.

News.title: Thousands of rail passengers hit by power failure disruption
News.content:
Thousands of rail passengers have described "nightmare" journeys, after being hit by delays and cancellations following a power failure at a signalling centre that caused major disruption across northern England.

A 90-second power outage occurred in the area covering Network Rail's Manchester Rail Operating Centre just before 14:00 BST on Thursday. The BBC understands there was then a delay to back-up systems kicking in, meaning affected trains had to stop while signalling was down.

Network Rail said "engineers are making good progress fixing the signalling issues" but warned that major disruption was expected until the end of the day on Friday.

At least eight rail operators remained affected on Thursday evening.

"We've got to really understand what's gone wrong here, because clearly something has and we've got to make sure we investigate that thoroughly to understand why things haven't restored as we would have expected," said Chris Wright, Route Director NW at Network Rail.

Network Rail said services may continue to be disrupted "because many trains and crews are not where they would normally be after this unexpected incident".

It has advised passengers hoping to travel on Friday to continue to check online for information on any further disruption, external: "As soon as we have information, we will keep you updated."

Manchester Rail Operating Centre was opened in July 2014 and houses all the controls to safely operate the railway in the region, including signalling.

According to Network Rail, its operational control boundary spans from Crewe in the south to Carlisle in the north, and from Todmorden in the east to the Welsh border in the west.

The initial power outage on Thursday afternoon was part of a wider power supply outage in the Ardwick area, but the BBC understands there was a delay to the back-up supply kicking in - which exacerbated the problem.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
More arrests have been made in Thetford as disorder linked to anti-immigration protests continued for a third night in the Norfolk market town.

A further two men in their 40s were arrested on Thursday evening, Norfolk Police said, taking the total number of people arrested in relation to the disorder to five.

One of the pair was arrested on suspicion of racial hatred, relating to offences on Wednesday, the force said. The other man was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and failing to give his details to police when asked.

Policing powers were stepped up in Thetford on Thursday evening following the disorder earlier in the week.

It came after police officers were "subjected to significant aggression" on Wednesday, including a female police officer who was "seriously bitten".

Crowds also attempted to storm homes linked to alleged asylum seekers on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings.

Police removed some people from a property on Thursday evening.

Amid the disorder, pictures appeared to show a heavy police presence in the residential area of Canterbury Way on Thursday night.

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

Norfolk Police has imposed public safety measures in the town, including requiring people to remove face coverings if asked to do so or face arrest.

They will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or who they suspect may commit, anti-social behaviour, to leave the area.

The measures were put in place from 18:00 BST on Thursday and remain until 07:00 on Friday.

News.title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
News.content:
Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cellsâ¦ this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

News.title: Village sees 50 days without rain during summer heatwave
News.content:
As the extremely dry spell continues across much of England and Wales, a small village in Surrey has notched up 50 consecutive days without rain this summer.

Wisley, most famous for being the site of the 240-acre garden owned by the Royal Horticultural Society, saw 36 continuous dry days back in the hot summer of 1976 - but has comfortably exceeded that number so far this year, with no rainfall since mid-June.

It comes after the driest July for England and Wales since Met Office records began 190 years ago, external.

Meanwhile, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued further yellow heat health alerts, external for most of England this weekend as the temperatures start to build again. The alerts cover the Humber, West and East Midlands, east of England, London, and the South East and South West from 09:00 BST on Saturday until 21:00 on Tuesday 11 August.

News.title: Amanda Knox defends Fringe comedy show after claims it will 'trivialise violence'
News.content:
Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has defended her solo comedy show following calls for it to be cancelled.

The sold-out show called Cartwheel, which Knox will perform at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, discusses motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter.

Knox told the BBC she is not the first person to use comedy to talk about traumatic events and said her material focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women".

But Stephanie Kercher, the victim's sister, said she is concerned it will "normalise and trivialise" violence against women, and Meredith, in particular.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Stephanie Kercher, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Responding to the comments, Knox said: "The interesting irony of that is that my daughter is a huge motivation for me doing this show.

"It's about how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women and what it means to raise a daughter in that world, knowing how bad it can be.

"If they [Kercher's family] saw my show, they would recognise that."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by nearly 5,000 people.

It states the show disrespects her memory and risks making light of such a harrowing event.

News.title: EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US firm
News.content:
No-frills airline EasyJet has agreed to be taken over in a Â£5.7bn deal by US firm Apollo after a rival bidder dropped out.

The takeover was agreed after US investment firm Castlelake, which had made a series of offers for the carrier, said it was withdrawing from the bid battle.

Apollo said it wants to help the airline grow and that it does not intend to cut any jobs in the first 12 months after the takeover has been completed, implying that passengers can expect largely the same service.

EasyJet is one of Europe's largest airlines. It employs more than 19,000 people, and flies around 1,200 routes across 35 European countries.

It was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer cheap air fares to Europe from the UK. Its first flights took off in November 1995 flying from Luton to Glasgow and Edinburgh, with its first international flights the following year.

Sir Stelios and his family still own around 15% of the business, and he said he supported Apollo's plans for the airline "to create more growth".

"My family and I intend to remain invested as long-term major shareholders of EasyJet for the next chapter in the company's journey," he said in a statement.

The future ownership of EasyJet has been uncertain since it emerged in late May that Castlelake was considering a bid for the airline.

Castlelake made a number of approaches for EasyJet, which were rebuffed initially after the carrier accused the US firm of trying to buy it "on the cheap".

In early July, EasyJet and Castlelake said they had agreed a deal in principle, but then Apollo - which owns Wagamama parent The Restaurant Group - swooped in with a higher bid.

Under the offer from Apollo, EasyJet shareholders will receive Â£7.15 per share.

AJ Bell's head of financial analysis, Danni Hewson said while the offer was significantly above where the company's shares were trading before the Iran war, the figure was "still woefully short of the company's pre-pandemic highs".

Apollo said it was "highly supportive" of the airline's existing strategy, adding there was "a significant opportunity to accelerate the operational and commercial ambitions" for the EasyJet Group.

"EasyJet is a leader in European aviation, having built a differentiated market position through its compelling customer proposition, expansive network and strong brand," said Alex van Hoek, partner and European private equity lead at Apollo.

EasyJet chief executive Kenton Jarvis said "We welcome Apollo's commitment to our business and our people, and believe that its experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for EasyJet."

The deal will still need to win approval from regulators, including in the EU where rules mean EasyJet's owners will have to be majority EU-based.

Apollo anticipates this can be achieved by making the Haji-Ioannou family, and other EU-based shareholders, owners of around half of the business.

Apollo said though it does not intend to cut any staff for at least 12 months after the deal goes through, if the deal completes and EasyJet delists from the stock exchange to become a private company, some jobs related to maintaining its public-listed operations could go.

The firm said that would be a "limited number of roles in specific areas."

AJ Bell's Hewson said the potential loss of another well-known name from London markets will be seen as a blow.

"Air travel might not be as sexy as space travel, but retail investors understand it and names like EasyJet can't easily be replaced," she said.

News.title: Boxer charged with killing aid worker in Greece after his wife gave police 'key' details
News.content:
Appearing in court earlier, Ahmadzai asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.

His lawyer, Christos Erdas, said his client had exercised his right to remain silent, and that his rights had been "violated" through leaks of evidence and documents from the case file - including his right to the presumption of innocence.

The lawyer said that when Ross was found, she had no injuries and any apparent cause of death was "entirely absent".

He said his client wanted the forensic medical report and the "toxicological and histological examinations of the deceased" to be included in the case file.

Erdas added: "His [Ahmadzai's] stance towards the prosecuting and investigating authorities did not constitute a stance of denial but, on the contrary, one of reservation, so that he may present his defence in full once the case file has been completed with the above essential documents â which were not sought by the preliminary investigating authorities â with the sole aim of establishing the substantive truth for both sides."

Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months.

News.title: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
News.content:
The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigned amid allegations of copying other academics' research.

Jason Arday's appointment in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment. Now, Cambridge says it has launched an investigation after "new information" emerged about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments.

There are two fundamental questions for the university.

Did it fail to adequately check Arday's credentials when appointing him, and did it defend that decision because of an institutional push to position itself as more diverse?

For one of the world's leading universities known for academic excellence and globally significant research, this is about its institutional culture and decision-making at the highest level.

The biggest reputational risk surrounds the accusations of academic plagiarism now under investigation - and denied by Arday - because they get to the heart of what a university is about.

The University of Cambridge uses the common definition of plagiarism as "passing off someone else's work as if it were your own without appropriate acknowledgement".

There is no allegation more serious that can be levelled at an academic.

One of the fundamental purposes of a research-led university is the creation of knowledge through original thinking, insights and inquiry.

The quality of this is the foundation of Cambridge's reputation, and a source of significant funding.

News.title: Met Police boss admits mistake over plagiarism row
News.content:
Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Grove said he had been investigating allegations Arday had plagiarised parts of his PhD, and contacted him in 2025 to offer him the right of reply.

"In early February I received a call from a Met police officer saying that a complaint had been raised against me by someone and Professor Arday was very distressed and I shouldn't contact him again," Grove told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was a complete shock. Apparently it was for harassment but I hadn't contacted him for four months and then maybe I think I've only sent three or four emails to him in total."

The Met closed its inquiries into the case.

Sir Mark told LBC: "We dropped the ball on that one, let's not beat around the bush.

"A report came in of harassment or some crime like that, it should have been screened out as not requiring investigation...

"We shouldn't have made that call to him [Grove] and said that."

The University of Cambridge said on Tuesday it had begun an investigation into Arday, who became the institution's youngest black professor in 2023, following "new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

In a statement published by campaign group Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said the "relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love".

"I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement," he said.

Speaking of his decision to step down he added it should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

His resignation followed a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis completed at Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) and other research.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, but did not uphold the charges.

The Times reported Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

In an interview with the Times, Arday said that he could not afford a proofreader to catch mistakes when he started out in academia.

Further questions were raised in the press about the truth of other claims, including Arday saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he raised Â£5.5m for charity.

News.title: Man wrongly jailed for murdering man wants to restore his 'forgotten' grave
News.content:
A man who was wrongly jailed for 11 years for murder is raising money to restore the grave of the man he was accused of killing.

Michael O'Brien was one of three men wrongly convicted of the 1987 murder of Cardiff newsagent Philip Saunders.

O'Brien, along with Darren Hall and Ellis Sherwood, became known as the Cardiff Newsagent Three. They were eventually cleared in 1999, in what became one of Wales' worst miscarriages of justice.

He said he recently visited Saunders' grave and was "sad" to see there was no longer a headstone there and the area was "unkempt."

"It just sort of hit home that one, the killer was still at large, and two, this man has largely been forgotten about," O'Brien said.

Saunders was killed with a shovel in his backyard. It seemed the ambush and brutal attack was an attempt to steal his day's takings.

In June, nearly 40 years on from the original crime, South Wales Police said they were launching a review of the evidence in the case, "in the hope advances in forensic science will provide the breakthrough needed".

News.title: Four men arrested after violent disorder near Pontypool, police say
News.content:
Four men have been arrested and two are in critical condition in hospital after violent disorder in south Wales.

The arrests were made following a disturbance involving a group of men in Pontnewydd, near Pontypool, at about 19:15 on Thursday evening, Gwent Police said.

Two of the men arrested are in police custody. In total, three men were taken to hospital for treatment.

Specially trained firearms officers and the National Police Air Service attended the scene, alongside paramedics, the force said.

Det Ch Supt Anne-Marie Salwey said: "Violence in any form is completely unacceptable and anyone who is found to be involved in this disorder will be dealt as we will not accept this behaviour in our communities.

"We recognise that reports of this nature will prompt concern from our residents and it is likely that you will see officers in and around the area conducting enquiries as part of this investigation," she added.

Police are asking for anyone with information, CCTV or dashcam footage from the area around Hospital Road and Mill Road between 19:00 and 19:30 on Thursday to contact them.

The road between Mill Road and Hospital Road is currently closed in both directions, with motorists urged to seek alternative routes.

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: All schools in England to get pupil attendance targets, government says
News.content:
Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve pupil attendance, the government has confirmed.

Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

It comes as official attendance data, published on Thursday, suggested school absence rates in England remained above pre-pandemic levels, with nearly one in five pupils missing at least 10% of school in the 2025/26 academic year.

Education minister Paul Waugh said the new attendance targets would take each school's local challenges into account, but that "every school has a role to play to improve attendance".

Before the Covid pandemic, when many schools closed to pupils for significant periods of time, attendance rates at English mainstream state schools regularly stayed above 95%, but schools have struggled to get back to those rates in the years since.

Thursday's figures, external suggested an overall attendance rate of 93% for 2025/26, a slight decrease on the previous year. That includes both authorised absences, such as illness, and unauthorised absences, which is when pupils miss school without permission or a valid reason.

The rates of persistent absence have doubled since the pandemic. A pupil is described as persistently absent if they miss at least 10% of school sessions.

In 2018/19, persistent absence rates for England state schools were around 10%, while the most recent data showed it was at 19% in 2025/26.

Pupils on free school meals and those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) were also still more likely to be absent from school than their peers.

News.title: Farmer jailed for lodger's 'body in barrel' murder
News.content:
A farmer who shot his lodger and dismembered his body has been jailed for 35 years.

Richard Dyson, 55, disappeared in November 2019, but his remains, kept inside a concrete-filled barrel in a trailer on a farm near Barnsley, were not discovered for nearly six years.

A trial at Sheffield Crown Court heard how Christopher Wright killed Dyson when he tried to steal a gun from him before disposing of the body with the help of his childhood friend Karl Schwalbe.

Last month, Wright, 73, was convicted of murder and Schwalbe, 72, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice.

Wright, a former butcher, was also found guilty of conspiracy to pervert the justice, preventing a lawful burial and six firearms offences.

Jailing him, Mr Justice Cotter said: "You had worked as a butcher and were skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for."

Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

Bethany Dainty, Dyson's daughter, said her life had become a "living nightmare".

She had issued numerous appeals for help tracing her father in the years he was missing.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, she said: "Someone watched me suffering for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand."

News.title: Woman charged after four stabbed near Covent Garden
News.content:
A 47-year-old woman has appeared in court after four men were stabbed near Covent Garden in central London.

Stella Gollovena, of no fixed address, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and one count of possession of an offensive weapon in a public place.

Police were called to Endell Street at about 12:30 BST on Wednesday after four men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 56, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to hospital with injuries that were not life-threatening or life-changing and have all since been discharged.

Gollovena appeared at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday afternoon where she spoke only to confirm her identity.

The incident took place in the capital's busy tourist area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants.

Police were "flagged down" by one of the injured men, the court heard.

London's Air Ambulance landed at nearby Trafalgar Square following the incident, although those wounded were taken to hospital by paramedics via road.

Four men provided statements to police, while a fifth person at the scene said they had also been stabbed but did not want to speak to officers.

Gollovena did not enter any pleas to the charges during the hearing.

She was remanded in custody and will next appear at Snaresbrook Crown Court on 3 September.

News.title: Calls for inquiry into Army teen college after reports of rape and abuse
News.content:
The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of AFC staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Ashleigh Percival-Borley, a veteran who served for 13 years in the British Army as a sergeant and multi-disciplinary instructor, said "incidents like this have "really taken my confidence out of the institution and that makes me really sad".

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there was a "level of frustration" from women who wanted to serve in the army.

She said hearing the allegations "sickened" her as a female veteran as well as a former instructor who knew "the embodiment of the army's values and standards" needed for the role.

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

The director of Spider-Man: Brand New Day has had an exceptional week, with his new film making $1bn (£742.3m) in just six days – but he’s also been left “heartbroken” by the cancellation of another Marvel project.

Earlier this month, Wonder Man – one of the best TV shows of the year – was cancelled by Disney+ despite being renewed for season two. Destin Daniel Cretton, who co-created the show with Andrew Guest, has now reflected on the unexpected news, hinting that the decision had nothing to do with Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige.

“I love that show to death,” he said in a new interview with The Wrap. “If it were up to me, we would be making that show. And I do believe that if – and I know this sounds weird – but if it were up to Kevin, we would be doing that show.”

open image in gallery ‘Wonder Man’ has been cancelled despite originally being renewed for season two ( Disney+ )

He continued: “And I’m just talking, I don’t fully understand the business of streaming, but if the business was right, we would be making that show because I know he loves that show as much as I do. It’s a bummer. I’m heartbroken about it. But I need to fully understand the why.”

In March, Wonder Man viewers were left overjoyed when Disney+ announced the Marvel series would be returning, branding the renewal a “small miracle” after streaming figures were lower than hoped.

However, Disney backtracked on its decision, with Variety reporting that the show’s writers have been released so they can pursue other projects.

When its first season was released, the satirical superhero show was hailed as being unlike anything Marvel had released in years, and received huge acclaim from viewers, not to mention a surprise Emmy nomination for lead star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II.

Abdul-Mateen II said of the cancellation news: “That’s life, right? Everything will shake out.”

He continued: “I wanted to say thank you to everybody who WATCHED the show, ENJOYED the show, and SHARED that they enjoyed the show in some way or other. The show worked. And that’s my favourite thing about it. So, thinking of you all today. I’m glad we got to be a part of something cool. Thank you for watching… And uhh… See you at the EMMYS.”

Wonder Man, which has 91 per cent on review aggregate site Rotten Tomatoes, follows Simon Williams, an anxiety-ridden jobbing actor who auditions for the lead role in the remake of the beloved superhero film Wonder Man.

open image in gallery ‘Wonder Man’ co-creator Destin Daniel Cretton directed new film ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ ( Getty )

He soon meets Ben Kingsley’s Iron Man 3 character Trevor Slattery, who may or may not have been recruited by the DODC (Department of Damage Control) to unearth a dangerous secret harboured by Simon. But before long, the pair strike up an unlikely friendship.

It’s been reported that the characters could return in other Marvel projects.

President Donald Trump went on a late-night posting spree on Truth Social on Thursday, sharing a Trump 2028 poster as well as images of himself inserted, apparently with the help of AI, alongside famous figures of American history.

One post featured Trump in military regalia alongside Generals George Patton and Douglas MacArthur, who served in World War II.

Others put the president alongside his famous White House predecessors.

In one image, Presidents Trump, Abraham Lincoln and George Washington all appeared to sign a map of the United States.

Another Truth Social post had Trump standing and laughing alongside President John F. Kennedy at Camp David.

open image in gallery President Trump mused about a third term and posted an AI image of himself as a general during a Truth Social spree on Thursday ( Donald Trump )

Perhaps most strikingly, the president used his post barrage to again float running for a constitutionally barred third term.

The Republican has often mused aloud or joked about a third term, including donning a Trump 2028 hat at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, though he has also said he’s aware he can’t run.

In the Oval Office on Thursday, President Trump again blurred the lines.

“We'll have a big percentage of the chip business by the time I leave office, which could be a long time,” Trump said. “Who knows? But it could also be fairly quick. They say two-and-a-half years. We're gonna find out."

In the same conversation with reporters, the president spoke about his thoughts on Vice President JD Vance’s potential 2028 campaign, describing the present as “too early” to make an endorsement.

In private, the president has reportedly told Republican donors he prefers Vance in 2028.

open image in gallery The president often wears a Trump 2028 hat, even though he has acknowledged he’s legally barred from seeking a third term ( AP )

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

The president’s allies have also offered mixed statements about a Trump 2028 run.

“It’s been a great run, but I think the president knows, and he and I’ve talked about the constraints of the Constitution,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters last year.

Podcaster and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon has said there’s a “plan” that would allow Trump to seek office again.

“He’s going to get a third term. Trump is going to be president in ‘28 and people ought to just get accommodated with that,” Bannon told The Economist in a video interview.

In October, the president admitted he can’t run for a third term, calling it “sad.”

Critics have accused the president of leaning into authoritarian tendencies through a variety of actions, including cracking down on the press, the use of masked immigration agents and the display of large banners of his face put over Washington government banners.

The Trump administration’s push to delay a ban on intoxicating hemp products could have a big benefit to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ son-in-law, according to new reports.

Last fall, President Donald Trump signed a spending bill to end the longest shutdown in history, which included a ban on hemp products containing certain amounts of THC, the main intoxicating compound found in cannabis. Now, the White House seems to have reversed course, reportedly pushing lawmakers on Capitol Hill to delay the very ban Trump enacted.

While the White House maintains that its new stance on the issue is in the interest of the American people, reports from The New York Times and MS NOW suggest that the move would allegedly benefit Wiles’ son-in-law, Bret Worley.

Worley, who married Wiles’ younger daughter Caroline in June, is the CEO of MC Nutraceuticals, a global supplier of hemp products. His company has been reportedly pushing industry allies to pressure lawmakers to delay the ban on hemp products, which is set to take effect on November 12.

In a new stopgap spending measure to avoid another shutdown at the end of September, senators added a provision delaying the implementation of the hemp product ban to December 11, reports say. The measure will be up for a vote this week.

open image in gallery The Trump administration’s push to delay a ban on intoxicating hemp products could have a big benefit to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ son-in-law, according to new reports ( AFP via Getty Images )

“The Chief of Staff has never lobbied in favor of this or any other position on hemp with Capitol Hill,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement to the media.

“The only interest guiding the Trump administration’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people, and the Administration continues to explore a Gold Science Standard-based framework on hemp to expand treatment options for American veterans and patients,” Desai said.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and Worley for comment.

As the spending measure was announced Sunday, MC Nutraceuticals said in an email to prospective buyers that the hemp industry now had “a seat at the table,” according to the Times.

Senator Ted Budd, a North Carolina Republican, has pushed against the delay of the hemp product ban, writing on X Monday, “I'm offering an amendment to the CR [continuing resolution] to strip out an extension of the hemp loophole to ensure unregulated, dangerous intoxicants are not sold, especially to kids.”

open image in gallery Bret Worley, who married Wiles’ younger daughter Caroline in June, is the CEO of a global hemp product supplier ( Getty Images )

The Food and Drug Administration wrote in an October 2024 notice that it was concerned about products containing delta-8 THC “in forms such as candy, chips, cereals and other foods that appeal to children.”

Budd told MS NOW that the White House’s new stance on the ban is “absolutely ridiculous.”

“We fixed this thing last year. We fixed it last November. They’ve had nine months to work on this, so why, all of a sudden, pop up for some seemingly innocent delay?” he said.

But Senator Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican, said the delay was worth it if it meant avoiding another shutdown. Last fall’s shutdown caused major airport disruptions due to staff shortages as agencies lacked the funds to pay government workers.

“I prefer that we don’t extend it, but I can live with a monthlong extension in exchange for keeping the government open,” Capito told the Times.

A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, to pay $567 million to address the harm its platforms have inflicted on young people. The ruling, part of the second phase of a landmark trial, brings the total penalty against the tech giant to $942 million.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid’s decision on Thursday allocates $420 million of the new funds to youth treatment services, with the remaining amount covering awareness, prevention, screening and other costs over five years.

The new penalty comes on top of the $375 million in civil penalties jurors ordered against Meta in March after finding that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms.

Prosecutors in this phase also sought fundamental changes at Meta, aiming to curb addictive features, improve age verification and prevent child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.

open image in gallery The new penalty comes on top of the $375 million in civil penalties jurors ordered against Meta in March a ( Reuters/Mike Blake )

Despite the size of the penalty, the $942 million total represents only a fraction of Meta’s projected annual profit, which is estimated at $60 billion in 2025. Investors largely shrugged off the ruling, with Meta’s stock falling less than half a percent to $589.44 in after-hours trading Thursday.

Still, the ruling is another setback for Meta, which faces an avalanche of lawsuits from thousands of families of children harmed by social media.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said it sends an unmistakable message that companies will be held accountable when their product designs knowingly put children at risk.

“Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online,” he said in a statement.

Meta vowed to appeal.

“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content," the company said in a statement. "We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.”

The look of Meta's platforms could change

The judge ordered Facebook and Instagram to build banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices and tools to address inappropriate comments, for example, and display them regularly. Those changes and an educational campaign in New Mexico would be subject to review by the state.

The court said federal children’s privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. The Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, means it cannot order Meta to request children to submit personal data or be passively tracked online, even for age verification purposes.

The court also noted that ordering verification of children’s ages only for Meta and not other social media companies would be “inequitable and unduly injurious” to the company.

open image in gallery The judge ordered Facebook and Instagram to build banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices and tools to address inappropriate comments ( PA )

Instead, the court ordered Meta to continue to improve its age assurance tools in New Mexico, which include using artificial intelligence to determine people’s age based on signals such as who their friends are and what types of content they post and consume. Meta must also attempt to develop a dedicated “under-13-years-of-age prediction model” in the next two years.

Additionally, Meta should also request proof of age for Instagram and Facebook users in New Mexico it estimates to be under 13. If it determines a user to be under 13, or under 18 but without being able to estimate a specific age, Meta must treat the user as under 13 or under 18 until the user verifies their age.

The company must also partner with schools or a child safety organization to create a reporting portal where school staff can flag users who may be under 13. And it must delete personal information it has collected on users under 13. The court also ordered Meta to report on its progress twice a year on how it’s complying with the abatement measures.

Meta is gearing up for a trial this month in California amid flood of lawsuits

Meta is also gearing up for a trial later this month in federal court in Oakland, California. Here, Meta will face the first four of 29 states that sued it in a federal multi-district lawsuit filed in 2023 for contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly designing features on Instagram and Facebook that addict children to its platforms.

Eight states, including Tennessee, where a trial is currently ongoing, filed lawsuits in their own state courts.

And late last month, Meta, along with TikTok, Snap and Google’s YouTube, were sued by the families of four teenagers who died by suicide over what they describe as “years of escalating harms” from using their platforms that eventually resulted in their deaths.

What comes out of New Mexico is the first of many dominoes that will fall for Meta, said Laura Edelson, an assistant professor at Northeastern University focusing on social media and cybersecurity.

“America is not going to pass a law that bans social media," Edelson said. "But if companies like Meta know they’re causing harm to users by product design, the states are finally finding a way to rein this in.”

News.content:

Lindsay Clancy sobbed uncontrollably Thursday as jurors were shown autopsy photos of her youngest child, whom prosecutors say she strangled in 2023, prompting the court to take an unscheduled break.

During the second week of her Massachusetts murder trial, prosecutors called additional witnesses, including friends, a former colleague and her former father-in-law, to testify about Clancy’s mental and emotional state. Many described her as open about her struggles with postpartum mental health issues while portraying her as a devoted mother who cared for her children.

Prosecutors are seeking to prove that the 35-year-old former labor and delivery nurse acted deliberately and should be held criminally responsible. Clancy’s defense argues she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a rare and severe psychiatric condition that can cause a loss of connection with reality after childbirth.

Clancy has pleaded not guilty to charges in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3 and Callan, 8 months, who were killed on Jan. 24, 2023, after she sent her husband out on errands. Prosecutors allege the trip was a plan to remove him from the home before the killings. Clancy remains paralyzed from the waist down after jumping from a second-story window of the family’s home that night.

open image in gallery CORRECCIÓN Juicio de Lindsay Clancy ( David L Ryan/The Boston Globe via AP )

A friend recalls a difficult reunion after the killings

None of the witnesses Thursday testified they heard Clancy express suicidal or homicidal thoughts. However, after the birth of her third child, she told them of trouble sleeping and harmful side effects from medications. She text-messaged one childhood friend to say medication had “caused her to have some dark thoughts.”

Amy Bevins visited Clancy in a rehabilitation facility after the killings. The two made small talk, she said, and played a game. When asked by prosecutors if Clancy brought up her children or cried about them, she said she had not.

But on cross-examination by Clancy's defense attorney, Bevins acknowledged the meeting was “awkward” and that Clancy's sister had said not to bring up the kids.

Lindsay Clancy's former father-in-law takes the stand

Christopher Clancy testified that he knew his then-daughter-in-law was having issues. At one point, he suggested the grandchildren stay with him and his wife, but his son declined.

“I knew she was having a hard time sleeping,” Christopher Clancy said. “I knew she just didn’t feel well. I knew she went to the emergency room where my wife was working. Those types of struggles.”

Clancy’s lawyers don’t dispute that she killed the children. But in the criminal trial and a medical malpractice lawsuit, her attorneys say she had bipolar disorder that wasn’t fully diagnosed until after the killings. Her attorneys say her condition seemed to worsen on the psychiatric medications, some of them problematic for bipolar patients.

If convicted of murder, Lindsay Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

open image in gallery If convicted of murder, Lindsay Clancy faces life in prison without parole ( CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via AP )

Another case that echoes Clancy’s is going back to court

Meanwhile, the judge and the district attorney learned Thursday that they face a retrial in another case involving a mother’s mental state when she killed her two school-age children in 2018.

Massachusetts’ top court threw out Latarsha Sanders’ murder conviction in the stabbings of sons Edson “Marlon” Brito, 8, and La’son Brito, 5.

Sanders told police in a recorded interview that she stabbed the boys because “bad people” text-messaged her commands to carry out a “ritual” connected to “Voodoo stuff” and the Illuminati. The latter is a purported powerful secret society at the center of various conspiracy theories, and Sanders’ family said she had become obsessively fearful of it.

Like Clancy’s lawyers, Sanders’ defense argued she was mentally ill and shouldn’t be held criminally responsible, while prosecutors said she acted deliberately. Prosecutors noted that Sanders tried to clean up the bloody crime scene, initially denied killing the children, and had written, in a disjointed personal notebook, about wanting to write books and become famous.

A defense neuropsychologist diagnosed Sanders with schizophrenia spectrum disorder, among other conditions, and testified that she was “grossly psychotic” when she killed the children.

The appeal turns on psychiatric evidence

The neuropsychologist was allowed to mention that he’d reviewed her medical records. But the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court faulted the judge for not letting jurors hear many specifics from the records, in which clinicians at a prison and a psychiatric hospital suggested similar diagnoses after Sanders’ arrest.

The doctors also noted that Sanders said she’d heard voices for decades, reported ongoing delusional and paranoid thoughts, and displayed odd behavior, such as licking windows.

Withholding the records from jurors “impermissibly stripped” the defense of its medical foundation, Justice Frank M. Gaziano wrote in a unanimous decision.

A message seeking comment was sent to a spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz, and messages were left for the judge, Superior Court Justice William Sullivan, through the court system.

Sanders’ lawyer, Robert F. Shaw Jr., welcomed the opinion and said he looked forward to retrying the case.

“The hope is that those records and that evidence will be able to be viewed by a jury with fresh eyes,” he said by phone. Sanders is in prison, and he hadn’t yet been able to meet with her to discuss the court ruling.

Her relatives told the Boston Globe last year that they hoped Clancy’s trial would generate more public scrutiny of Sanders’ case.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.title: Woman with sepsis sues Chipotle after eating bowl she claims had salmonella-linked peppers
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. A woman who was hospitalized with sepsis has sued Chipotle after eating a burrito bowl she claims had salmonella-linked jalapeño peppers.

Kristen Behne got sick after eating at a Chipotle restaurant in Roseville, Minnesota, on June 24, her lawsuit claims.

“Three days later she was in a hospital bed, febrile, tachycardic, and septic—a life-threatening complication of the Salmonella infection caused by Chipotle’s grossly contaminated food,” read a lawsuit filed on Behne’s behalf against the Mexican food chain Wednesday.

Federal health officials have linked a recent Salmonella outbreak to jalapeño peppers from Mexico that were distributed to Mexican restaurants in the US, including Chipotle and Qdoba.

As of Wednesday, 345 people from 27 states have been infected with the outbreak strain of Salmonella, and there have been 36 hospitalizations, according to data collected by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Minnesota and Colorado have been hit the hardest, with more than 100 cases each. There have been no outbreak-related deaths reported.

open image in gallery A woman who was hospitalized with sepsis has sued Chipotle after eating a burrito bowl she claims had salmonella-linked jalapeño peppers ( Getty Images )

The Food and Drug Administration says people were infected with the foodborne bacteria for about a month starting on June 19. Of the nearly 200 people that officials interviewed, 93 percent reported eating at a Mexican restaurant before getting sick, including Chipotle and Qdoba, according to officials.

Behne’s lawsuit claims that she was one of the people “poisoned” by Chipotle. Her lawyers argue that the Salmonella sample recovered from her body matched the strain that caused the outbreak.

“Ms. Behne did nothing wrong. She could not have inspected her food for Salmonella; the pathogen is invisible, odorless, and tasteless,” the lawsuit read. “She was entitled to rely—and did rely—on Chipotle’s representations that the food it prepared and sold was safe to eat. Those representations were false.”

Chipotle switched its jalapeño supplier for the stores that were impacted by the outbreak starting on July 20, and Qdoba also stopped serving the peppers about a week later.

“The health and safety of our guests and employees is our highest priority,” Chipotle said in a statement Wednesday.

The company said it has a “robust ingredient traceability system and, upon learning of a potential Salmonella outbreak in the supply chain impacting wholesalers and restaurants,” it identified the affected jalapeños, “proactively removed them from the restaurants where they had been distributed, and replaced them with product from different growers.”

The FDA says it does not believe there is an ongoing risk from Chipotle and Qdoba because they removed the affected jalapeños. The Independent has reached out to Chipotle and a lawyer representing Behne for comment.

open image in gallery Over 300 people have been infected with Salmonella from jalapeño peppers sourced from Mexico, according to federal health officials ( Getty Images )

Common symptoms of salmonella infection are watery diarrhea, stomach cramps and fever. But there are also more severe symptoms, and patients could have long-term complications.

On June 27, Behne started getting symptoms such as fever, chills and vomiting, according to the lawsuit. She lost consciousness at one point and had a temperature of 102 degrees, her lawyers said.

The next day, Behne “experienced more than ten episodes of diarrhea in a twenty-four-hour period,” the lawsuit said.

She was admitted to the hospital on June 28 and discharged two days later.

But Behne “continues to experience the effects of her acute Salmonella infection and her septic episode,” and she is “at increased risk” of complications, including reactive arthritis and post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit seeks more than $75,000 in compensatory damages.

People are also seeking legal action against Taco Bell amid the cyclospora outbreak that has infected more than 10,000 people across the country this summer.

More than 500 infected people have been hospitalized, and two patients with underlying medical conditions have died, according to officials. Federal health officials have linked the outbreak to Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce sourced from Mexico and sold at Taco Bell.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.
