World.title: Alternative-fuel passenger vehicles fast catching up with petrol ones
World.content:
Passenger vehicle retail sales increased 19% year-on-year to 4.1 lakh units, crossing the four-lakh mark for the first time in July

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Alternative-fuel passenger vehicles are on the verge of overtaking petrol-powered models in India, with CNG, hybrid and electric vehicles accounting for 40.6% of passenger vehicle retail sales in July, just behind petrolâs 41.7%, according to data released by the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) Thursday. The gap has narrowed sharply from 13.2 percentage points a year ago to just over a percentage point, reflecting a rapid shift in buyer preferences.The trend came as Indiaâs automobile retail market recorded its strongest-ever July performance, with overall registrations rising 25.8% year-on-year to a record 25.9 lakh units. For the first time, all six vehicle categories â two-wheelers, passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles, three-wheelers, tractors and wheeled construction equipment â posted their highest-ever July retail volumes, underscoring broad-based demand across the industry.Passenger vehicle retail sales increased 19% year-on-year to 4.1 lakh units, crossing the four-lakh mark for the first time in July. Within the segment, CNG vehicles accounted for 24.6% of sales, hybrids for 8% and electric vehicles for 7.9%. While hybrid vehicles continue to use petrol as their primary fuel source, automakers classify them as alternative-fuel vehicles because they combine an internal combustion engine with an electric powertrain to improve efficiency and reduce emissions.Petrolâs share, meanwhile, declined to 41.6% from 47.6% a year earlier. FADA said fresh model launches, affordability gains following GST changes and consumersâ increasing focus on lower running costs supported demand for alternative powertrains. The dealersâ body also noted that uncertainty surrounding the transition to E20 fuel appears to have nudged some buyers towards CNG, hybrid and EVs.The transition was equally evident in the two-wheeler market. Electric two-wheelers accounted for a record 11.2% of retail sales in July, up from 7.7% a year earlier.Overall EV retail registrations across all vehicle segments climbed to an all-time high of 3.28 lakh units during the month, taking EV penetration to about 12.7% of total vehicle retail sales from 9.6% a year ago. Maruti Suzuki retained its lead in the PV market in July, retailing over 1.6 lakh units.

World.title: Survey: 81% of study-abroad aspirants plan to return home
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The foreign degree may be global, but the career plan is largely homeward-bound: 81% of Indian study-abroad aspirants surveyed by Oxford International said they planned to return to India after completing their courses.

Nearly nine in 10 were the first in their family to pursue education overseas, while almost half said the decision to go abroad was their own.

The findings are part of the third edition of Student Global Mobility Index, which combines 17,925 responses to core questions with about 2,400 responses to additional questions on courses, family background, information sources and post-study plans. Another 15% chose "applying for job" as their next step, without indicating whether the job would be in India or overseas.

The biggest shift over three survey cycles is in who drives the decision. Self-motivated students rose from 29% in 2023-24 to 34% in 2024-25 and 49% in 2025-26. Family influence fell from 59% to 37% and then 36%. Younger students were more likely to rely on family guidance, while older applicants tended to decide independently. Self-motivation was highest in north and south India; family influence was strongest in the west and central region.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





Academic choices were heavily concentrated. Seven in 10 were applying for postgraduate courses, and 75% identified business and management as their main field. Health and medicine was a distant second at 8%. Sciences accounted for 2% and engineering 1%.

Google searches led 39% of students to their institution, followed by agents (35%). But Google's lead widened on trust: 56% named it their most trusted source for education information, compared with 20% for college events and 9% for Instagram. AI tools were trusted most by 6% and YouTube by 5%.

World.title: Temporary disability cert no bar for PwBD quota MBBS seat: NMC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Candidates cannot be denied admission to MBBS courses under the PwBD quota solely because they hold a temporary disability certificate or Unique Disability Identity (UDID) card, National Medical Commission (NMC) said.

However, it made it clear that their disability status will continue to be verified by medical assessment boards (MABs) before they are declared eligible for counselling.

In an addendum to "Guidelines on Assessment of Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) for Admission to the MBBS Course, 2026", NMC Wednesday said the change has been made to ensure that the guidelines are interpreted in line with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, 2024 Rules and a 2025 office memorandum issued by the department of empowerment of persons with disabilities.

Under the revised norms, candidates whose disabilities are categorised as progressive, non-progressive or not likely to improve will not be denied admission merely because their UDID card or disability certificate is temporary. Their disability status, however, will continue to be verified by designated MABs before an eligibility certificate is issued. Candidates holding temporary UDID cards whose disability has been recorded as "likely to improve" will undergo reassessment before their eligibility is decided.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





MABs will also assess each candidate's functional competency.

"This year's revised guidelines unnecessarily created a new hurdle by introducing a distinction between temporary and permanent disabilities. I received multiple representations from students who were being harassed at assessment centres in Agartala, Mumbai and Delhi. That prompted us to submit a representation to NMC and raise this issue in the ongoing SC hearing as well," disability rights activist Prof Satendra Singh said.

NMC said the addendum has been issued to ensure uniform implementation of admission guidelines and should be read as an integral part of the July 27 notification.

World.title: Settling with a few cases won't stop CBI probe: Supreme Court warns realtors
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has put a spoke in efforts of defaulting realtors to escape CBI probe by settling with a few homebuyers. The court said these builders would continue to be investigated for cheating homebuyers and siphoning off their deposits till the last of the flat purchasers get their property or refund.

Many homebuyers had become parties to petitions filed by groups of homebuyers pleading similar cause â enormous delay in project completion by builders who have already received money through banks under subvention and the banks insisting on repayment in disregard of the fact that the flats are yet to be delivered.

Many bank officials found to have colluded with realtors, Supreme Court told

Advocate Pranav Sachdeva told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the court may allow those homebuyers, with whom defaulting builders has settled, to withdraw from petition and continue proceedings for the remaining homebuyers left high and dry by builders.

Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for CBI, informed that the agency had completed probe in 18 of 50 cases in which CBI registered FIRs on SCâs orders. A total of 17 chargesheets and a closure report have been filed before competent courts.

She said the chargesheets name several bank officials who were found to have colluded with builders. The agency has invoked provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act against them and CBI has sought sanction to prosecute the officials from State Bank of India, Bank of India, Uco Bank, HDFC and ICICI.





SC said in court monitored investigations, sanctions for prosecution should be granted promptly and directed these banks to give necessary permissions within two weeks for prosecution of the accused bank officials. âFailure to accord sanction within two weeks would require banks to submit explanations to the court,â it said and asked CBI to share documents on money trail to ED for initiation of inquiry under PMLA.

On some complaints regarding alleged defaulting builders in other states, across states, the bench directed the CBI to conduct a thorough investigation into the allegations of misrepresentation and other irregularities by entities such as Ozone group in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu; Vivansaa in Bengaluru; Rudra Buildwell Pvt Ltd in Greater Noida, and Omaxe group in Chandigarh. A separate status report in respect of investigations into these builders and related banking institutions shall be submitted to the court.

The main allegation, as crystallized by amicus Rajiv Jain, against these builders is that they donât have ownership title over the land and have partnered leaseholders to construct housing projects. However, they advertised as if they owned the land, entered into agreements with homebuyers and financial institutions without the lessee being a part thereof and remained unaccountable for delay and default.

Given the expanding workload, Bhati informed SC that CBI had sought additional hands from states for expediting the investigations but none of the states have responded to the CBI directorâs request. The bench directed the DGPs of UP, TN, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Punjab to send on deputation required number of personnel, as requested by CBI, within 10 days.

World.title: DMK lays down conditions to support delimitation Bill
World.content:
As the Narendra Modi government explores the possibility of bringing in a constitutional amendment Bill to carry out a fresh delimitation exercise, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) may consider extending support if the government revises the legislation bringing in three essential changes to the Bill that reached the Lok Sabha in April.

There is a freeze on seats based on the 1971 Census which ends after the latest Census that is expected to be completed in 2027. The DMK wants this constitutional freeze to remain for another 25 years, while amending the Constitution to introduce a 50% blanket increase in the Lok Sabha seats for all States, which was verbally promised by Home Minister Amit Shah when the legislative package aimed at bringing about delimitation was brought in Parliament in April.

Additionally, the party wants a Schedule of the number of seats that each State will have in the legislative package, as per sources in the DMK. A top DMK leader said that the government has not yet approached them on the issue either “formally or informally”. The party maintains that it will take a final call only once the form and substance of Bills are known.

These conditions come amid renewed efforts from the government to reach out to the Opposition, with Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju speaking to Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi again on Thursday. “I had a productive conversation with Rahul Gandhi. I have made a request on a few specific issues and also discussed other matters. We expect continuous communication and coordinated action with the Congress and other Opposition parties,” Mr. Rijiju said.

The Parliamentary Affairs Minister had also met Mr. Gandhi at the latter’s office in Parliament on Wednesday, during which the Congress leaders are also said to have reiterated their opposition to any constitutional amendment to carry out the delimitation exercise.

Though the government doesn’t have the two-thirds majority yet to push through a constitutional amendment, the political situation has changed since April 17, when the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill was defeated on the floor of the House. The numerical strength of the INDIA bloc has since vastly changed.

In the present 540-member Lok Sabha, the two-thirds majority mark is 360, and if 22 Lok Sabha members of the DMK vote for the Bill, the government’s strength would go up to 346. While the government would still be short of 14 MPs, the threshold changes if there are abstentions during the proceedings. If the government brings the Bill to the Rajya Sabha, it will find it easier to reach the two-thirds majority mark. In the Rajya Sabha, if all 244 members are present during voting, the government needs 164 votes. The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance currently has 158 MPs.

Mr. Shah had earlier said that once it is assured of the numbers, the government would once again bring the constitutional amendment Bill to increase the strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 seats in order to implement the 33% reservation for women after fresh delimitation.

Since April, the government has secured the support of 20 rebel Trinamool Congress MPs, who are now part of the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) and six Shiv Sena MPs who had switched sides from the Uddhav Thackeray faction to the Eknath Shinde-led faction.

On Friday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be hosting the NCPI and Shiv Sena MPs for a breakfast meeting.

In anticipation of the delimitation and the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bills coming up next week, the Congress is all set to issue a three-line whip, asking its members to be present in Parliament next week.

Meanwhile, the Lok Sabha continued to be disrupted over the Opposition protests regarding police action against students.

Speaker Om Birla started the proceedings in the morning by commemorating the anniversaries of the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and members stood in silence to pay tribute to the victims.

Thereafter, Opposition MPs began raising slogans, demanding the presence of Mr. Shah in the House over the police action against student protesters on July 20. Some members were also seen displaying placards.

World.title: How Beijing innovates: Lessons from China’s market-state hybrid model
World.content:
If the conventional wisdom about innovation is that it is best left to individuals and private enterprise — and the best thing a government can do is get out of the way — that is certainly not the thinking in Beijing.

How innovation happens in Beijing offers a snapshot into China’s model in which research universities, start-ups, the market and the state all have a role to play.

The Chinese capital has always had the country’s most important cluster of research universities, with Peking University and Tsinghua leading the list. It is also home to several cutting-edge robotics and AI companies, including Moonshot, which was started by graduates of Tsinghua and made waves over its latest Kimi K3 open-source model.

“A closed loop from project discovery to incubation” is how Yang Xiuling, who as the Director General of the Beijing Municipal Commission of Development and Reform leads the city’s top economic planning body, describes the ecosystem. “Our greatest strength,” she says, “is talent and the concentration of top research universities.”

The challenge that then follows is how to leverage that talent, or, as she puts it, “how to move results out of the lab”. The gap between translating early research into commercially sustainable ventures is known as the “valley of death” for innovation. To cross that valley in Beijing, the state steps in.

Beijing’s Zhongguancun research cluster is at the forefront of tech innovation in China, along with clusters in Shenzhen, Shanghai and Hangzhou. A strong undercurrent of competition underpins the national innovation ecosystem, especially when it comes to attracting and keeping talent.

To deal with the “valley of death”, Beijing set up what it calls “an intelligent platform for results commercialisation” led by a group of tech managers, who, Ms. Yang says, “are a bridge because they understand both the tech and the market”. In 2025, the city’s platform executed 1.04 lakh tech contracts.

“Markets and companies are still at the centre,” Ms. Yang says. “But the way we look at it is that the companies pose questions, and the universities can provide answers. The companies still play a key role in R&D and in taking the lead in collaborative research with institutions”.

The universities provide the foundation from which the rest follows, says Zhang Jihong, who is a Director at the state-run Zhongguancun Science Park. “It’s the universities that have helped incubate a number of high-tech enterprises,” he says. “We have formed a virtuous cycle where the universities produce talent, the talent provides intellectual support for innovation, and innovation again reinforces the growth of universities.”

The state as investor

The state’s role here is twofold. It provides the hard infrastructure, as seen in the science park and a number of incubators littered around Zhongguancun.

More importantly, it also provides capital, not only linking start-ups to private venture capital (VC) but also stepping in with state-backed capital to help bear some of the risk.

The state taking a direct stake in companies is a unique feature of this ecosystem. The upside is it helps bear losses and allows for the longer-term, patient kind of support that VC might not afford. This has played a key role in enabling the speed and scale of innovation in China.

The downside is wasteful spending, if state funds do not do their due diligence, which is often the case. So much so that this has emerged as a growing concern for Chinese regulators, who in June issued new rules to tighten how local governments spend these funds.

The intense competition among different clusters, coupled with the collapse in land sales as a source of revenue for local governments, has led to a splurge in spending at the local level, with each province putting in funds with the hope of finding its national champions, even if they lack the capacity to do the needed due diligence. The new rules have now called for stricter control over how these funds are spent and for more approvals from the Central government.

Humanoids on the factory floor

AI and robotics are the twin peaks of Beijing’s current innovation drive. If Zhongguancun in the north is the home of tech talent, the Yizhuang industrial cluster in the city’s southern suburbs offers a snapshot of how innovation is playing out on the factory floor. Here, a hub-and-spokes model has the state’s Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre at its centre, which funnels talent to a number of robotics companies around its periphery. “The idea,” explains Che Zhengping, who is Head of Embodied AI at the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, “is to build a full supply chain that is ready for mass production”. The current focus in humanoids is to “shift from industrial use scenarios to daily use scenarios”, including healthcare, which is expected to be a major source of demand in an ageing society.

Among the companies in Yizhuang is Lingyi iTech, which in April started production on humanoid robots and is already planning to scale up. “Advancements in technology are making it more affordable” to scale, says Vice President Philip Yang. “As we move from semi automation to full automation,” he estimates, “costs in 2030 will be half of what they are today.”

Lingyi already has production capacity “for the next 5 to 6 years”. By the end of 2027, it will be making 20,000 robots annually. The plan is to scale up to 1 lakh units by 2028 and 5 lakh by 2030 from this Yizhuang facility (the company has four others), by when it hopes to be “one of the world’s top three”.

At the state-run innovation centre next door, researchers pore over unfinished humanoid robots, getting them to perfect a range of delicate movements before the latest model is given the green light.

State subsidies of land, policy and tax support are among the more well-known elements of China’s industrial policy. The state’s enabling of talent and intellectual support are perhaps less well-known, but arguably just as important when it comes to getting innovation right.

World.title: Saudi military says Houthi attacks left 11 civilians, including child, injured near Yemen border
World.content:
More than 10 civilians, including a 4-year-old child, were injured in Saudi Arabia on Thursday (August 6, 2026) after a series of attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, according to the Saudi military.

West Asia LIVE: Houthi missile attacks kill 58 Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, says source

The attacks, which took place in the southern region of Najran, near the Yemeni border, came hours after the Iran-backed rebels claimed responsibility for another series of strikes in central and eastern Yemen that killed at least 30 government troops and wounded at least 50 others.

A Houthi leader said Saudi-backed troops were targeted in the attacks and that “hundreds” were either killed or injured. The assaults hit camps for forces of the internationally recognised government in the provinces of Marib and Hadramout, the Yemeni officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

Turki al-Malki, a spokesman for the Saudi military, said the later attack wounded seven Saudi nationals, one Yemeni, two Egyptians and one Pakistani expat. The Houthis did not release any statement.

“The terrorist Houthi militia carried out these terrorist attacks using indiscriminate shelling against civilian objects, which is a flagrant violation of the Customary International Humanitarian Law through deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian objects,” Mr. al-Malki said in a post on X.

The back-to-back attacks mark the latest major escalation since a de facto truce in Yemen in April 2022 that halted major fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition, which backs the internationally recognised government.

Yemen's army reported publicly only that the Houthi attacks on its camps had left dead and wounded among its troops, but it didn't give a death toll.

Houthi Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the attacks on camps in Marib and Hadramout provinces were carried out with ballistic missiles and drones and that they were in response to a build-up of Saudi-backed forces in eastern Yemen.

The strikes killed and injured “hundreds of Saudi enemy mercenaries” and destroyed and burned camps, depots, military vehicles and weapons, the Houthi leader said.

“We call upon all our people to remain vigilant and confront any Saudi aggression, and to strike Saudi troop concentrations wherever they may be,” Houthi leader Saree said in his address.

The U.S. mission to Yemen expressed condolences to the families of the killed Yemeni soldiers in Hadramout and Marib, adding in a statement on X that the attacks by the Houthis “represent yet another example of their terrorism against the Yemeni people.”

Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa, forcing the internationally recognised government into exile in Saudi Arabia.

A Saudi-led coalition intervened months later and has been battling the rebels since 2015 to try to restore the internationally recognised government to power. However, the war has turned into a stalemated proxy conflict with neither side winning.

The Houthis claim that their recent escalation, including a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is in response to the Kingdom's air and sea blockade on Yemen since 2015.

World.title: J&K Police file FIR over PDP’s Article 370 anniversary rally, party says ‘blatant misuse of power, authority’
World.content:
The J&K police on Thursday (August 6, 2026) lodged a First Information Report (FIR) against the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) leaders and workers, two days after the party took out multiple street protests over the abrogation of Article 370 in Srinagar. The PDP termed the FIR against the party leaders as “a blatant misuse of power and authority”.

The name of former J&K Chief Minister Mufti has been mentioned in the FIR for taking out a rally on August 4 and August 5 in the city, on the seventh anniversary of the abrogation of Article 370, “without prior police permission”, a senior PDP leader said, on the condition of anonymity.

The FIR also mentioned the name of Ms. Mufti’s daughter, Iltija Mufti, who led a late-evening street protest in Lal Chowk on August 4 and was stopped by the police. The FIR against Ms. Iltija Mufti is lodged under Section 132 (assaults on a public servant), 121 (Voluntarily causing hurt to deter public servant from his duty) and 191 (2) (political rallies and mob violence).

Officials said a police party visited the residence of Ms. Mufti in Khimber in Srinagar, pertaining to the case on Thursday (August 6, 2026) evening.

According to the FIR, the workers of the PDP, led by PDP president Mehbooba Mufti and Iltija Mufti, started moving towards the main road (on August 4). “Police personnel requested them not to assemble on the main road, as such a gathering could disrupt the smooth movement of traffic. The request was not well received by the workers of the PDP. Instead, they turned aggressive and attacked the police party,” said the FIR.

It said the PDP workers criminally used force against the police party, “obstructed them in the discharge of their official duties, and also resorted to pushing and manhandling”. “As a result, several police officials sustained injuries,” it added.

Ms. Iltija Mufti said the FIR was “an attempt to intimidate the PDP to normalise abrogation of Article 370 like the National Conference (NC)”. “No rioting broke out at the site. We wanted to march to the city centre and peacefully organise a sit-in over abrogation of Article 370. A police officer Neha Jain dragged me and manhandled me in spite of being a woman herself. She goaded other police personnel to manhandle me,” Ms. Iltija.

She said the police permission was a pretext to clamp down. “It’s unfortunate IPS officers from outside are imposed on people of J&K. Mere displaying placards with Article 370 on it is being treated as sedition. There is no freedom of expression. I have been protesting since 2019, but have never come across such a police officer or policing,” said Ms. Iltija.

She accused the police of erasing the CCTV footage from the shops nearby. “If the police have nothing to hide, why was CCTV footage erased from nearby shops? The police should make the entire CCTV footage public,” she added.

Meanwhile, a PDP spokesman said the FIR by the police against Ms. Mufti and Ms, Iltija Mufti on Article 370 “was a blatant misuse of power and authority”.

“The woman police officer assaulted the PDP leader and used excessive force while preventing her peaceful protest. We have eyewitnesses to the incident and intend to place the matter before a court of law,” said the PDP.

The party said such actions by responsible police officers are “illegal, disproportionate, and wholly uncalled for”.

“We strongly condemn the conduct of the police personnel involved and demand appropriate action against those responsible for allegedly manhandling a political leader during a peaceful protest,” the PDP said.

World.title: National Handloom Day: Inside the Bonda tribe’s enduring Ringa weaving tradition
World.content:
“Every Ringa we weave carries our family’s story,” says Muduli, gently running her hand over the striped cloth she has just taken off the loom in Gokharipada village of Odisha’s Malkangiri district.

The Ringa is the traditional handwoven garment worn by Bonda women as a wraparound skirt. Woven with striking horizontal stripes with bands of red, maroon, black, white and blue, it has long been an emblem of the Bonda tribe, one of India’s Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs).

Living in the Bonda Hills of Malkangiri district, the community has safeguarded its language, customs and weaving tradition over generations. In this matriarchal society, women carry forward much of that cultural memory, preserving the art of weaving even as the modern world steadily reaches their remote villages.

Anthropologists believe the Bondas are descendants of one of the earliest waves of modern humans to leave Africa nearly 60,000 years ago, though this remains a subject of ongoing research. Their language, Remo, distinct customs and attire have endured despite increasing contact with the outside world. The Bondas accord women a central place in family and community life. Women cultivate crops, collect forest produce, negotiate at the weekly Thursday shandy and preserve traditions such as weaving, passing them from one generation to the next.

Every Thursday, women from villages such as Gokharipada descend from the hills to the weekly shandy at the Onukudelli market. Layers of brightly coloured bead necklaces cover their torsos, aluminium neck rings gleam in the sun, blue shawls draped across their shoulders and the handwoven Ringa wraps around their waist.

From kerang to cotton

Historically, the garment was woven using fibre extracted from the Kerang tree (a small wild shrub native to the Eastern Ghats). Cotton yarn gradually replaced bark fibre as markets became more accessible, although the visual identity of the textile has remained largely unchanged.

“What makes the Bonda weaving tradition unique is that it has always been closely tied to the community’s identity rather than to commerce,” says Navaldeep Thareja, a textile engineer from Sangrur in Punjab. Over the past several years, he has travelled to little-known weaving and craft clusters across India, documenting textile traditions that seldom find space in mainstream conversations. Through his initiative, Behrupiaa Arts, he has recorded the stories of artisans whose creations are deeply rooted in local culture and organises curated tours for visitors.

“Unlike many handloom traditions in Odisha that evolved around markets, the Bonda community wove the Ringa primarily for personal use. It is one of the few textile traditions where a single garment has remained central to the community’s identity for generations.”

The fabric is tightly woven and is durable. “This is because it was created as everyday clothing rather than ceremonial attire,” Navaldeep explains. Within Bonda households, weaving has never existed as a specialised occupation. It fits into the rhythm of daily life alongside farming, gathering forest produce and household responsibilities.

Muduli recalls that she first learnt weaving by observing the women in her family. “Like most Bonda girls, I watched my mother and the elder women weave from a young age.” Mothers guide daughters, while grandmothers quietly correct mistakes until muscle memory takes over. The loom, therefore, functions as much as a family archive as it does a tool for producing cloth.

A single Ringa generally takes two to three days to complete, depending on the yarn, the design and the time available after daily chores. “We weave whenever we find time between household work and farming,” she says.

Unlike many weaving clusters that create saris, shawls or home furnishings for wider markets, Bonda artisans traditionally produced only the Ringa. “It was never meant for large-scale production,” says Muduli. “We mostly wove it for our own family and community.”

That pattern is gradually changing. Visitors, textile scholars and collectors increasingly purchase Ringas directly from artisans, providing a modest supplementary income. Some buyers display them as framed textile art, wall hangings or table runners.

Keeping tradition alive

Before every visit to a Bonda village, participants joining Navaldeep’s textile tours receive detailed briefings on local customs, photography etiquette and appropriate behaviour. Groups remain deliberately small and interactions take place only when community members are comfortable.

“We never treat the village as a tourist attraction,” he says. “The purpose is to create understanding while respecting the community’s privacy.” Artisans who wish to engage with visitors often bring their woven Ringas to locally managed homestays instead of opening private homes to tourists. This arrangement allows conversations to unfold naturally while giving weavers complete freedom to participate on their own terms.

Yet the future of the craft is not without uncertainty. “The biggest challenge is that weaving alone does not provide a steady income,” Muduli says. “Many young people are choosing education and other jobs. Everyday clothing has also changed over time, so fewer young women are learning weaving regularly.”

Ready-made garments have become commonplace. Even so, the Ringa continues to occupy an important place within the community, especially during traditional festivals when families gather dressed in their customary attire.

Muduli welcomes the growing appreciation shown by visitors because every purchase carries encouragement beyond its monetary value. “It makes us happy that people appreciate our weaving and our traditions. When someone values the Ringa, it encourages us to continue this craft and pass it on to the next generation.”

Behrupiaa Arts conducts textile tours to Malkangiri. For details, contact 9953097898.

World.title: The hands that are shaping Amaravati
World.content:
Cranes and earthmovers dominate Amaravati’s skyline as Andhra Pradesh’s greenfield capital, where towering government complexes and landmark infrastructure, takes shape. But behind the rapid construction is a quieter story of migrant workers, local communities, women exploring entrepreneurship and skill development opportunities, and the people whose lives are being transformed alongside the city.

Among the thousands of workers contributing to Amaravati’s transformation is 46-year-old Deepak Maiti from Purba Medinipur district of West Bengal, who has spent the past year amid cranes, concrete, and steel helping build the capital city.

Maiti is among 1,900 migrant labourers, mostly from West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, and Odisha, engaged in constructing the sprawling multi-storied NGO housing project at Nelapadu village under Thullur mandal in Guntur district. His workday begins early and stretches for nine hours. Despite demanding schedule, thoughts of home are not far away. “My old mother awaits me back home. I visit her whenever possible,” he says softly.

As dusk settles over the workers’ camp, the atmosphere begins to shift. After a long day at the construction site, labourers gather around carrom boards and ludo games, sharing laughter and enjoying moments of camaraderie. Yet, conversations often drift back to families waiting thousands of kilometres away.

Maiti’s story is echoed by many others at the site, each carrying a similar tale of migration, sacrifice and hope. One of them is 35-year-old Indrabhan, a farmer from Bharatpur in Uttar Pradesh, who arrived in Amaravati four months ago in search of additional income, while the crop on his farm awaits harvesting.

“Like many seasonal migrant workers, I plan to return once the farming season demands my attention,” he says. On a lighter note, he adds that five fellow workers from his home State are also at the site. “I don’t feel out of place, and adapting to life in the camp has been easier,” he says.

Inclusivity

To make life away from home easier for these migrant workers, the contractor has put in place facilities to cater to their diverse cultural and daily needs. Separate kitchens and dining areas allow them to prepare meals according to their culinary preferences, while a grocery store within the camp stocks daily essentials, lending a sense of familiarity and routine to life far from home.

The camp site is equipped with bunk beds, sanitation facilities, safe drinking water, kitchens, dining halls, first-aid centres, CCTV surveillance, emergency response systems and recreational spaces for sports and weekend movie screenings.

Even with these facilities, the emotional burden of migration remains difficult to overcome. For 32-year-old Ramswamy from Odisha’s Rayagada district, separation from family remains the hardest part of life away from home. Having arrived in Amaravati six months ago in search of work, he left behind his wife and two young children, an eight-year-old son and a two-year-old daughter. After a long day at the construction site, one ritual remains non-negotiable. “I make video calls every day after returning to my room. Seeing my children refreshes my body and heart,” he says, a gentle smile lighting up his face. “The facilities here do not lessen the pain of separation from the family,” he adds.

Life at the site is not entirely defined by work and separation. Community celebrations, including birthday events, provide workers with relief from the rigours of construction.

Welfare at the camp extends beyond accommodation and recreation. ”Welfare measures complement a safety programme that begins even before a worker enters the site,” says Nilanchala Hotta, Occupational Health and Safety Manager at Larsen and Toubro, the multinational conglomerate company implementing the NGO housing project.

Highlighting the mandatory medical examinations, safety induction, and continuous training, Hotta says the project has recorded four million safe work hours while maintaining full compliance with environmental and social safeguard standards.

Beyond work

The scale of these measures becomes evident when viewed against the backdrop of Amaravati’s massive construction activity, stretching over expansive tracts of land. The rich alluvial plains, once known for their fertile agricultural fields nourished by the River Krishna, now bear the unmistakable marks of large-scale excavation and earthwork.

Every few kilometres, fleets of earthmovers, excavators, bulldozers, graders, dump trucks, and compactors dot the landscape, their steady movement underscoring the scale of activity under way. The roads tell the story of a city being built from the ground up. Traffic slows as signboards caution motorists with messages of “go slow”, “deep excavations in progress,” “heavy machinery at work,” and “construction zone ahead.”

Beyond the heavy machinery and construction sites, efforts have been made to support the families who have migrated with the workforce. Snaking around excavation sites will lead to a crèche set up at a labour camp in Thullur, where P. Swathi, the caretaker, is surrounded by nearly 30 children in the 3- to 10-year age group.

Bridging the language gap with the children is a challenge, shares Swathi, who is a native speaker. “I try to communicate with them in my broken Hindi,” she says with a sheepish smile and a shrug.

Caring for children is only one part of the broader social support system. Persuading mothers to send their children to the crèche is a difficult task, says Ch. Nithisha, a gender specialist deployed by the Social Welfare wing of the Andhra Pradesh Capital Region Development Authority (APCRDA). “Attendance remains an uphill task,” she adds.

Beyond childcare, efforts are also being made to address gender concerns, enhance safety, and create opportunities for women through dedicated welfare and empowerment initiatives. Describing her role, Nithisha says it entails preparing and implementing a Gender Action Plan, conducting awareness programmes, and providing training on gender issues and gender-based violence prevention.

She is also responsible for establishing grievance redressal mechanisms, supporting women’s livelihoods and entrepreneurship, and ensuring that the project’s benefits are inclusive, equitable, and responsive to the needs of women and vulnerable groups. “We have established Internal Complaints Committees at all levels of the projects,” she says, adding that she visits camps where women migrant workers live to see if they feel comfortable.

“Women take time to open up, and it is important to ensure their welfare while they work far away from their homes,” she says.

Bridging the gender gap

While migrant workers play a key role in Amaravati’s construction, the city’s development is also reshaping the lives of local communities that once heavily depended on agriculture. For generations, farming was the primary source of livelihood for families across the villages that now make up the Amaravati Capital Region.

Even as many landowners voluntarily pooled their land for the construction of the new capital, the need for alternative sources of income became increasingly important. Employment opportunities remained limited, particularly for women, owing to low literacy levels, early marriages, and socio-cultural norms that largely confined them to their homes.

Recognising this gender gap, the APCRDA has been working to make local women active participants in Amaravati’s growth story. “The CRDA’s Entrepreneurship Development Programme equips women with vocational skills, business training, and market linkages, enabling them to establish micro-enterprises and generate sustainable livelihoods,” says Col. V. Ramulu, Group Director of CRDA Social Development Wing.

“Through this programme, we are helping women become economically independent,” says Ramulu. The initiative aims not only to improve household incomes but also to empower women to become stakeholders in the development of the State’s future capital.

One such outcome of these efforts is the promotion of women-led entrepreneurship through “Amaravati Amma Vanta” initiative—a community-based food brand developed by the CRDA to promote local livelihoods and the culinary heritage of Andhra Pradesh. “This initiative supports women Self Help Groups (SHGs), local producer groups, and micro-entrepreneurs by providing training, quality standardisation, branding, packaging, and market access for traditional food products such as millet-based foods, pickles, sweets, snacks and other value-added local specialties,” Ramulu says.

The impact of the initiative is reflected in the journey of Adineni Mahalakshmi, a 21-year-old from Mandadam village, who had no understanding of the concept of financial independence. A Class VII dropout, she is now considered one of the successful micro-entrepreneurs. Mahalakshmi says, “I never thought I could contribute meaningfully to my family income.” As a homemaker, Mahalakshmi sells millet malt, which is in great demand among CRDA employees and people visiting the office for grievance redressal.

Mahalakshmi’s success story is one among many that highlight the programme’s wider impact on women’s livelihoods in the capital region. The initiative began with millet-based food processing training for 161 community members, leading to the establishment of 26 women-led micro-enterprises, with each entrepreneur now earning an average monthly income of ₹12,000. Encouraged by this success, APCRDA plans to expand into dairy products, culinary powders, pickles and other traditional foods under the “Amaravati Amma Vanta” brand.

“We are also exploring partnerships with corporate market facilitators such as HESA Global to connect these enterprises with organised retail outlets and wider markets, ensuring long-term commercial sustainability and improved livelihoods,” says Mr. Ramulu.

“Amaravati Amma Vanta” is only one among several livelihood initiatives being promoted in the capital region. The focus is also on equipping women with marketable skills that can pave the way for self-employment and entrepreneurship.

This is evident in the beautician training classes being conducted at an auditorium on the SRM University-AP campus. The classroom buzzed with enthusiasm as participants eagerly learnt professional beauty and grooming techniques, many nurturing dreams of setting up home-based salons or small enterprises that could provide them with a steady source of income.

Nearly 100 women from villages across the Amaravati Capital Region sat engrossed as trainer G. Vasavi demonstrated beauty and skincare techniques. The beautician course, offered by APCRDA in collaboration with SRM University-AP, is one of several skill development programmes designed to equip local residents with employable skills and encourage entrepreneurship.

“I would love to start my own beauty business from home after completing this course,” says Kaithepalli Sravani, a homemaker from Thulluru. Then, breaking into laughter, she adds, “Even if I don’t get any customers, I can at least use what I’ve learned to enhance my own beauty.”

For Borra Sri Durga Shanti, a young mother of two from Malkapuram, the training represents an opportunity to contribute to her family’s income. “I can’t wait to start my own beauty parlour and support my husband financially,” she says.

“These women are quick learners and constantly ask questions that go beyond the course curriculum,” says Vasavi, a cosmetologist and makeup artist. As part of the tie-up, SRM University is also conducting training programmes in Fitness and Nutrition Science, GST and Tally, cybersecurity, digital marketing, embedded systems, and Very Large Scale Integration technology for various sections of the local community. Additionally, a free weekly Ayurvedic medical camp, organised at the APCRDA Project Office with the support of the Department of AYUSH, provides consultations and medicines to employees and farmers visiting the capital region.

Social and environment

The focus on inclusive development transcends livelihoods and extends to the environment as well. The officials’ effort to ensure that urban development goes hand in hand with environmental conservation is exemplified by the centralised tree translocation facility, which has been developed on 15 acres of land in Anantavaram.

This facility preserves mature trees that would otherwise be lost to infrastructure development. Nearly 10,000 trees representing 54 species are being scientifically relocated, rehabilitated, and nurtured before being replanted across Amaravati’s future parks and avenues. Instead of waiting decades for new saplings to mature, the initiative safeguards existing canopy cover, biodiversity, and carbon sequestration, ensuring that the city’s green heritage grows alongside its urban infrastructure.

From protecting decades-old trees to creating spaces for remembrance and farewell, Amaravati’s development story is rooted in a broader vision of care, sustainability, and human dignity. A multi-faith funeral campus in Amaravati is a first-of-its-kind integrated facility designed to provide dignified, affordable, and environmentally sustainable funeral services for people of all faiths.

The campus addresses the lack of adequate funeral infrastructure in the capital region by offering religion-specific spaces and common amenities such as prayer halls, cremation and burial facilities, a mortuary, waiting halls, a dining area, parking, and landscaped grieving spaces. “The project was planned after extensive consultations with religious leaders and community representatives and aims to cater to the city’s needs for the next 15 years while serving as a model that can be replicated elsewhere,” says Mr. Ramulu, noting that the ₹13-crore project, built on 6.89 acres in Thulluru, has been completed and is ready for inauguration.

While construction machinery continues to dominate the skyline of Amaravati, officials are ensuring that development remains socially and environmentally accountable. In many ways, the foundations for the new capital are being laid not just with concrete and steel but also with the aspirations of the people building it.

World.title: Govt mulls bypassing Zardari’s assent for judges’ appointment
World.content:
• President has yet to approve summary for JCP-recommended hirings

• Govt reviewing possibility of issuing notifications under Article 48(1)

• Presidency sources warn bypassing procedure may lead to complications

• IHC reserves verdict on maintainability of plea challenging delay in notifying appointments

ISLAMABAD: The federal government is considering notifying the appointment and confirmation of high court judges despite President Asif Ali Zardari not having formally accorded assent to the recommendations made by the Judicial Commission of Pakis­tan (JCP), sources told Dawn.

The JCP, during its meetings held on July 20 and 21, recommended the appointment of 19 additional judges to the high courts, confirmed the services of four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court and one additional judge of the Lahore High Court, and extended the tenure of an additional judge of the Sindh High Court by six months.

However, the appointments have yet to be notified by the Ministry of Law and Justice as the president has not formally approved the summary.

According to informed sources, the government is examining the possibility of invoking Article 48(1) of the Constitution to issue the notification, arguing that the president was required to act on the summary within a fortnight of its submission.

Since that period has expired, they believe the government may proceed with the appointments.

The sources said the delay had already created practical complications.

Four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court, whose services were confirmed by the JCP, ceased to hold office after the exp­iry of their tenure on Aug 4 due to the absence of a formal notification.

Similarly, an additional judge of the Sindh High Court, whose tenure had been extended by the JCP for another six months, also relinquished office after his term expired on July 29.

When contacted, Minister of State for Law and Justice Barrister Aqeel Malik said the government would resolve the matter within the constitutional framework and in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Constitution and the principles laid down by the superior courts.

However, sources in the Presidency cautioned against bypassing the prescribed procedure, warning that any such move could trigger political and legal complications.

They said Articles 48(1) and 48(2), which define the respective constitutional roles of the president and the prime minister, as well as Article 175A(8), which deals with the appointment of judges, left room for differing interpretations.

According to Presidency sou­rces, any ambiguity should be resolved through mutual consultation between the president and the prime minister rather than through unilateral action.

On the other hand, government sources maintained that judicial appointments were governed by constitutional provisions and that any deadlock must be resolved strictly in accordance with the Constitution.

IHC reserves verdict on plea

The Islamabad High Court reserved its verdict on the maintainability of a plea challenging President Zardari’s delay in approving a summary for the appointment and confirmation of judges to various high courts.

The writ petition, filed by advocate Luqman Zafar Chaudhary through his counsel Zahid Asif Chaudhry, urged the court to direct the president to approve the summary forwarded by the prime minister for the judicial appointments recommended by the JCP.

Justice Arbab Muhammad Tahir took up the plea on Thursday, with the petitioner’s counsel arguing that the JCP had recommended the appointments during its meetings on July 20 and 21.

He contended that the summary had reportedly not been approved by the president even after 15 days had passed.

The petitioner’s counsel told the court that reports suggested the government might issue notifications for the appointments in the next 48 hours.

During the hearing, the contents of his client’s plea were also read out on the court’s direction, and Justice Tahir repeatedly questioned whether a constitutional petition could be maintained against the president.

He asked the counsel to cite any precedent in which a writ had been issued against the president.

The court also observed that the judgements cited by the petitioner did not support the proposition advanced by his counsel for issuing directives to the president.

The court asked the lawyer to identify any decision in which a court had issued directions to the president regarding the exercise of powers under Article 48 of the Constitution.

Article 48 states that the president shall act “on and in accordance with the advice of the cabinet or the prime minister”. However, it adds that the president can ask the cabinet or the PM to reconsider the advice within 15 days of receiving it and shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration within 10 days.

Sources in the Presidency have contended that the provision also empowered the president and did not set a timeframe for appointments. They cited its second clause, which states: “The president shall act in his discretion in respect of any matter in respect of which he is empowered by the Constitution to do so.”

However, legal experts have noted that the SC had previously held that the president lacked discretion in appointing superior court judges and must follow the PM’s advice.

The petitioner’s lawyer argued that notifications for judicial appointments were usually issued by the law ministry after the president’s approval, but the ministry could issue them even without presidential assent.

He contended that the president’s role in the process was ceremonial and that if approval was withheld, the competent authority should proceed with issuing the notification. After hearing his arguments, the court dec­lined the request to issue notices at this stage and rese­rved its decision on the maintainability of the petition.

World.title: Pakistan working with partners to defuse Hormuz stand-off: FO
World.content:
• Says Oman, other ‘brotherly states’ leading different aspects of diplomacy

• Insists Islamabad is focused on settlement rather than ‘individual symptoms of crisis’

• Pakistan examining TORs, operational modalities of Saudi-led maritime coalition

• Govt will decide on Gaza stabilisation force after formal proposal

ISLAMABAD: The Foreign Office on Thursday insisted that Pakistan remained actively engaged in efforts to defuse the Strait of Hormuz stand-off, while also examining the terms of reference and operational modalities of a newly announced Saudi-led multinational maritime coalition aimed at protecting shipping routes in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

The Foreign Office acknowledged that different regional partners, particularly Oman, were taking the lead on different aspects of the diplomatic process. It portrayed Islamabad’s role as part of a coordinated effort by “brotherly states” to steer the crisis back towards the framework established under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).

“Pakistan remains engaged alongside other brotherly states in sincere efforts to resolve the crisis in the Gulf and the Middle East, especially with respect to the stand-off in the Strait of Hormuz,” Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir And­rabi said at the weekly media briefing.

He explained that the current phase of diplomacy involved a division of responsibilities among regional actors.

“Pakistan is playing the role. We remain engaged with the parties. Obviously, on certain issues, there are countries that take the lead, and on certain other issues, there are other countries that take the lead,” he said.

The remarks came as Oman assumed the lead role in negotiations with Iran over the future management of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a process mandated under Article 5 of the Islamabad MoU signed between Tehran and Washington in June.

That provision required Iran to ensure temporary toll-free passage for commercial shipping before entering into negotiations with Oman and other Gulf littoral states on the future administration of navigation, maritime services and related arrangements.

High-level Iranian-Omani talks began days after the MoU was signed and have since evolved into a series of technical and political consultations on shipping routes, maritime services, cost-sharing and other operational issues.

Iranian officials this week said substantial progress had been achieved, including agreement on the geographical coordinates of a proposed shipping route, although differences over operational control, service charges and related matters continued to be discussed.

Seeking to place Pakistan’s role within that broader diplomatic effort, Mr Andrabi said: “Overall — if you look at the comprehensive efforts undertaken by Pakistan, Qatar and other brotherly countries, you will see a very coordinated and concerted facilitation process. This was particularly on the Strait of Hormuz.”

He drew a distinction between Pakistan’s role during periods of acute crisis and its longer-term engagement in the overall diplomatic process.

“You need to understand that the Strait of Hormuz was a stand-off, and in such a stand-off, dialogue was essentially the paradigm of facilitating a settlement,” he said.

“Mediation is a more long-term process. The question of mediation comes when you are addressing issues that require persistent deliberations over a period of time, as, for example, the events leading up to the Islamabad MoU, the Pakistan-Qatar Joint Statement and the technical-level talks that it envisages,” he added.

The explanation appeared aimed at underscoring that while Oman, as one of the two littoral states bordering the strait, now occupies the central role in negotiating its future management, Pakistan continues to view itself as an integral participant in the diplomatic effort that produced the Islamabad MoU and the subsequent implementation framework agreed with Qatar.

Reaffirming Islamabad’s continued engagement, Mr Andrabi said: “Pakistan remains engaged, and, as I said, this is a concerted teamwork and coordinated effort from the brotherly countries, including Pakistan. We value the partnership of our brotherly countries in this regard.”

“We will continue these peace efforts in concert with our brotherly countries and partner countries,” he added.

The spokesperson also suggested that Pakistan’s immediate focus remained on securing implementation of a political understanding rather than becoming involved in negotiations over specific manifestations of the crisis, including the blockade and attacks on commercial shipping.

On a question about the Strait of Hormuz blockade, he said, “We are more engaged with the settlement and less so with terms of the crises. The blockade is one facet or symptom of the crisis. Once the agreement is reached and implemented, these symptoms of the crisis, either blockade or accidental/voluntary attacks on maritime traffic, will obviously take care of themselves. So, therefore, the agreement is important, and this is where our focus is.”

Saudi-led maritime coalition

Mr Andrabi told the weekly media briefing that the Saudi-led multinational maritime coalition remained at an evolving stage and the government was consulting military authorities before taking any decision.

“Regarding this maritime security arrangement (announced by Saudi Arabia), the process is evolving. We are seeing what the terms of reference will be and how this security arrangement will function,” he said.

“We are in touch with our Naval Headquarters and the military authorities on this issue, and on how these modalities will work out,” he maintained, adding that the coalition’s eventual composition also remained uncertain.

Saudi Arabia announced the coalition on July 30 following a meeting in Riyadh attended by military representatives from 43 countries.

Conceived as a collective maritime security framework for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, the alliance seeks to safeguard commercial shipping and energy routes against escalating threats, particularly after Yemen’s Houthi rebels declared a maritime blockade against Saudi shipping and subsequently claimed attacks on commercial vessels.

Pakistan was among the founding endorsers of the initiative, reflecting its long-standing strategic partnership with Riyadh, although the Foreign Office comments indicated that Islamabad was still assessing the alliance’s practical framework before determining the extent of its participation.

Saudi authorities maintain that the arrangement is purely defensive, operates in accordance with international law and leaves participation in operational activities to the sovereign discretion of member states.

Its activities are expected to include intelligence sharing, joint exercises, capacity building and coordinated maritime security operations.

The spokesperson’s remarks came as Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif departed for Saudi Arabia on a three-day official visit. Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir is also expected to join him.

Saudi Arabia on Thursday also appointed Rear Admiral Abdullah bin Salem Al-Shehri as the first commander of the coalition, completing its initial leadership structure ahead of a planners’ meeting scheduled for Aug 12 and 13 that is expected to finalise operational arrangements and facilitate additional accessions.

Islamabad also indicated that it would decide on joining the proposed International Stabilisation Force for Gaza only after receiving a formal proposal, suggesting that discussions on Pakistan’s possible contribution remained at a preliminary stage.

Responding to a question, the spokesperson said: “As regards future peacekeeping, peace-enforcement or peace-making forces in Gaza, I think that question is a bit premature. When a proposal or a proposition to that effect is presented before us, a decision will be taken accordingly.”

World.title: Govt reduces petrol price by Rs3.19, high-speed diesel by Rs1.50
World.content:
The government on Thursday reduced the prices of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.19 and Rs1.50 per litre, respectively.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs329.82 per litre while HSD will cost Rs382.36 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs110 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs96 per litre on HSD.

The Petroleum Division’s notification said the new prices would be applicable for August 7 (Friday).

The diesel price has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Ex-Afghan general, agent’s pleas against arrest, deportation rejected
World.content:
• Petitioners cite fear of Taliban persecution if sent back to Afghanistan

• Peshawar High Court notes fears of detention and removal don’t constitute valid cause of action

• Rules immigration, visa and residency matters fall within executive’s domain

PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court (PHC) has rejected petitions filed by a former general of the erstwhile Afghan National Army and a special agent of the former Afghan Presidential Protective Service (PPS), along with their families, seeking protection against their imminent arrest and deportation by law enforcement agencies.

A bench comprising Justices Wiqar Ahmad and Kamran Hayat Miankhel dismissed two almost identical petitions filed by former general Baryalai Sharifi and former PPS special agent Abdul Mujeeb Ghairat and their family members. They had approached the court fearing persecution by the Taliban government in Afghanistan if deported.

The counsel for Mr Sharifi submitted that his clients were Afghan nationals who had entered Pakistan on valid visas.

He claimed that Mr Sharifi had served as a general in the former Afghan National Army (Milli Urdu) and that he and his family had received threats from the present Afghan regime.

He added that Mr Sharifi’s wife had served as an assistant doctor in the PPS of the former Afghan government, while his son claimed to have worked as a training camp guard in the same service.

The counsel further stated that Mr Sharifi had approached the Society for Human Rights and Prisoners’ Aid (SHARP) for pre-screening in connection with an international protection and resettlement process, and apprehended that the petitioners might be arrested or deported from Pakistan.

‘Mere apprehension’

“The petitioners have not challenged any specific order, notification or action of the respondents adversely affecting their legal or fundamental rights,” the bench observed in its four-page written order.

“The entire case rests upon a mere apprehension that they may, in future, be subjected to arrest, detention or deportation. Such speculative apprehension, without any concrete cause of action or demonstrated violation of law, does not furnish a valid ground for invoking the extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction of this court under Article 199 of the Constitution,” it added.

The court observed that “matters relating to the stay of foreign nationals in Pakistan, grant, extension or cancellation of visas, and their immigration status are governed by the relevant statutory framework and fall within the exclusive domain of the competent executive authorities”.

“Any request for international protection, refugee processing or resettlement through SHARP, UNHCR or any third country does not, by itself, create an enforceable legal right against the respondents capable of being enforced through a constitutional petition,” it held.

Similarly, in the case of Mr Ghairat, counsel submitted that the petitioner and his family were residing in Pakistan on valid visas and had applied online for their renewal.

He stated that Mr Ghairat had served as a special agent in the former PPS, an elite US-trained security unit responsible for the close protection of the then Afghan president.

The counsel argued that owing to his previous service under the former Afghan government, Mr Ghairat and his family would face danger if returned to Afghanistan.

He contended that in view of the ongoing action against certain Afghan nationals, the petitioners feared arrest and deportation despite their claimed lawful stay in Pakistan.

“The questions relating to the petitioners’ right to remain in Pakistan, renewal or extension of visas, or their immigration status fall within the exclusive domain of the competent executive authorities under the relevant immigration and foreigner laws,” the bench observed.

“In the absence of any unlawful action, refusal of a statutory request, or infringement of a vested legal right, no writ can be issued directing the respondents to grant protection or confer a legal status upon the petitioners.”

Published in Dawn, August 7th, 2026

World.title: Daily flights to Riyadh from 14th
World.content:
KARACHI: Saudi Arabia’s new national carrier, Riyadh Air, has announced an expansion of its routes to Pakistan, with daily flights connecting the two capitals set to commence on August 14.

In a statement, the airline said that ticket sales had started for the Islamabad-Riyadh and Lahore-Riyadh routes, while the inaugural service to Lahore would be launched on August 18.

A total of seven flights per week would operate between Riyadh and Islamabad, while the Lahore route would be served by three flights per week, the statement said.

The airline said that the new routes will be operated on Riyadh Air’s new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, featuring the airline’s latest cabin interiors and on-board experience. The Dreamliners feature four cabins, including Business Elite, Business, Premium Economy and Economy class.

The Lahore-Riyadh and Islamabad-Riyadh routes have been planned to offer smooth onward connectivity to Europe and the Middle East, catering to both business and leisure travellers from Pakistan, the statement said.

World.title: Pakistan to emulate Chinese techniques of investigation
World.content:
• Naqvi says centre in Islamabad will combine detention, investigation and summary trial facilities under one roof

• Initiative aims to speed up disposal of minor offence cases, reduce procedural delays

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is set to embark on a major transformation of its policing system, with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi announcing a series of reforms inspired by successful international law enforcement models, including the establishment of a China-style Law Enforcement Investigation Centre in Islamabad.

The announcement came during his meeting with assistant superintendents of police who recently returned after completing specialised training courses in China and Turkiye.

The officers described overseas programmes as an invaluable experience that significantly enhanced their professional capabilities and exposed them to modern policing practices, surveillance technologies, and contemporary approaches to maintaining law and order.

Acknowledging the importance of international exposure, Naqvi declared that foreign training programmes would become a permanent component of the professional development of Pakistani police officers. He emphasised that the government was committed to equipping the country’s law enforcement agencies with the skills and technologies required to address emerging security challenges.

As part of the reforms, the interior minister announced the launch of a pilot project to establish a China-style Law Enforcement Investigation Centre in Islamabad.

The centre will integrate detention, investigation and summary trial facilities under one roof, enabling the swift and efficient disposal of cases involving minor offences while reducing procedural delays.

Naqvi said the country would benefit from internationally proven policing models to make its law-enforcement system more effective, responsive, and technology-driven.

He stressed that the adoption of advanced surveillance systems and modern technologies would significantly expand monitoring capabilities and strengthen crime prevention efforts.

To further enhance public safety, the interior minister announced that modern drones would be inducted into the Aviation Wing of the Ministry of Interior to improve surveillance and support law enforcement operations.

The reform agenda also includes strengthening investigative capacity through the establishment of specialised investigation rooms at the National Police Academy.

According to the interior minister, greater emphasis will be placed on specialised investigation training aligned with the evolving requirements of modern policing.

He further announced that interrogations would be introduced as a specialised academic subject within police training, with modern interrogation techniques based on the practices of developed countries becoming an integral part of the curriculum.

In another key initiative, Naqvi revealed plans to introduce new police uniforms designed to better meet the operational requirements of law-enforcement personnel, reflecting the practical demands of contemporary policing.

During the meeting, the ASPs shared their observations on advanced policing systems in China and Turkiye, highlighting the effective use of surveillance technologies, modern equipment, digital tools, and public security management practices that could be adapted to Pakistan’s policing framework.

The Commandant of the National Police Academy, the Director General of the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), and other senior officials also attended the meeting.

World.title: PTI remains wary as govt renews talks offer
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: While the government has once again invited the main opposition party, PTI, to begin negotiations, the party has linked any dialogue with improved meeting facilities and access to medical care for its founding chairman, Imran Khan.

Aamir Dogar, the PTI’s Chief Whip, met National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq on Thursday. The meeting was also attended by Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry.

Speaking to the media after the meeting, Dr Fazal said the government had once again offered talks at the venue proposed by PTI within Parliament House. “The ball is now in PTI’s court,” he said, expressing hope that the opposition would respond positively.

He recalled that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had earlier offered dialogue to the opposition, but PTI had not responded.

Aamir Dogar meets NA speaker, minister in Parliament House

He said negotiations were the only way to resolve political issues.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram, while talking to Dawn, confirmed the meeting but said the situation was not as simple as presented by the government.

He claimed the National Assembly session was scheduled to begin on Aug 7, but PTI had not received any formal intimation regarding it. He added that Aamir Dogar approached the National Assembly Secretariat to inquire why the party had not been informed about the session.

According to Mr Akram, the secretariat informed Mr Dogar that the NA session had been delayed until Aug 17, alleging that the government did not want to bring the ongoing tensions and allegations between the PML-N and PPP into parliament.

He said the National Assembly Secretariat later informed Mr Dogar that Speaker Sadiq wanted to meet him. During the meeting, the speaker also invited Dr Fazal and conveyed that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had twice offered dialogue, but PTI did not respond.

Mr Akram said PTI made it clear that negotiations could not take place unless a conducive environment was created. He said the party had demanded permission for meetings with Imran Khan and access to his personal doctors. “Otherwise, we cannot sit with the government merely for photo sessions,” he added.

He said the speaker also suggested that PTI join parliamentary standing committees; however, the party conveyed that any decision on the matter would be taken by Imran Khan.

Mr Akram said the government now had to respond positively if it wanted negotiations to move forward.
