World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Commonwealth's PFAS case against 3M 'daunting', judge says
World.content:
A Federal Court judge has described the Commonwealth's $2 billion lawsuit against the chemical manufacturing company 3M over PFAS contamination at defence bases as "daunting".

During the first case management hearing in Federal Court today the two parties agreed the Australian government's claim was "large and complex".

It heard a 1,600 page statement of claim has been filed about alleged soil and water contamination at 28 defence bases across Australia, where firefighting foam containing PFAS chemicals was used.

Justice Catherine Button told the court sitting in Melbourne she had "never seen a claim like this … and to characterise it as daunting would be an understatement, daunting for everybody".

3M Company has manufactured PFAS chemicals since the 1950s. (Supplied: 3M)

In March the Commonwealth announced it was seeking damages from US-based chemical manufacturer 3M and 3M Australia.

It the largest legal claim ever brought by the federal government, attempting to recoup the costs associated with investigating, managing and remediating contamination from the legacy use of AFFF firefighting foam.

It alleges the company withheld the results of its own environmental laboratory testing that shows there were significant adverse environmental effects associated with its PFAS products.

3M released a statement saying "we will defend ourselves against these claims through legal process", and despite ceasing the sale of the products at issue in Australia two decades ago the Department of Defence continued to use them.

The Commonwealth is seeking damages from the manufacturer of a firefighting foam that contaminated 28 defence bases. (ABC News)

3M has faced a number of lawsuits over PFAS contamination across the globe.

In 2023 it settled a $US10.3 billion ($14.5 billion) claim with a number of American public water providers to test for and treat the substances but did not admit liability.

'Retired, if not dead, by the time it comes to trial'

Fiona McLeod AO SC, representing the Commonwealth, told the court that while the bases have been and continue to be remediated the PFAS compounds "persist in the environment and do not breakdown".

She said the case references research conducted by 3M, including an historical study on monkeys which showed the chemicals were persistent and toxic to animals.

In an effort to expedite the matter Ms McLeod suggested the respondents plead to the claims relating to six defence sites selected by the applicant before the end of the year.

She told the court those bases included a mix of environmental issues they have encountered, including where contamination plumes are stagnant, where safe drinking thresholds are being exceeded and where PFAS continues to migrate.

Justice Button agreed with the approach to select certain sites that would help identify issues between the parties.

"This matter can't run on a traditional set of train tracks otherwise we'll never get there," she said.

"We'll all be retired, if not dead, by the time it comes to trial".

The STOP PFAS group has identified firefighting foam used at a petrol tanker crash in 1992 as the main source of contamination. (Supplied)

King's Counsel Philip Solomon for 3M told the court it had a large legal team dedicated to the case, including four barristers.

He said it was the "most complex matter I've ever seen" and suggested that it might have taken then Commonwealth two to four years to prepare its 1,600-page claim, which Ms McLeod denied.

When asked by Justice Button what the "big picture" defence would be, Mr Solomon said while it was still working on a "master list" it had "obvious elements of complex science", including five limbs on liability and four limbs on causation.

Justice Button ordered the matter to return to court on October 16, by then the parties will have agreed to which number of bases 3M will enter pleas to in full.

3M must file and serve their defence on December 11.

World.title: Melbourne's deputy lord mayor poised to become Liberal Party candidate
World.content:
Melbourne's deputy lord mayor, Roshena Campbell, is almost guaranteed a seat in the Victorian Parliament after being chosen to replace Moira Deeming on the Liberal Party ticket.

The party's state executive last night selected Ms Campbell, a barrister, to run on the top of the Liberal ballot for the upper house in the Western Metropolitan Region this November.

She beat out current MP Trung Luu, who had the support of senior Liberals in parliament.

Roshena Campbell was previously unsuccessful as the Liberal candidate for Aston in a 2023 by-election. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Mr Luu will have to reapply for the second position on the ballot, which is generally winnable but which will come under serious threat from One Nation.

Ms Campbell is considered a talent who could quickly enter the frontbench, but she does not live in the electorate that covers communities from Footscray to Sunbury and Werribee.

She previously ran in the 2023 Aston by-election but unexpectedly lost the seat for the federal Liberals, in what was a historic victory for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Deeming exit prompts new Liberal ticket

The Liberal Party was forced to reopen the contest for Western Metropolitan Region candidates after unanimously revoking Ms Deeming's preselection.

Ms Deeming had accused her party room colleague and former opposition leader Matthew Guy of putting her in a headlock at a crowded community function.

Police reviewed CCTV of the interaction and said no offence was detected.

But Ms Deeming refused to apologise, saying she made the allegation in good faith.

She was disendorsed as a result but remained a member of the parliamentary Liberal Party before taking herself to the crossbench last month.

Moira Deeming has since moved to the crossbench after months of rancour between herself and the Liberal Party. (AAP: Diego Fedele)

Ms Deeming's husband, Andrew Deeming, wrote on social media that the party's decision to select Ms Campbell showed "contempt" for the west.

Once elected in November, Ms Campbell would need to resign from her position in local government. The Municipal Association of Victoria (MAV) also advises state and federal election candidates to take a leave of absence from their council no later than the date of their nomination.

Liberal Party preselection for the ticket had already been a shambles.

Ms Deeming initially lost the preselection to Dinesh Gourisetty. But he was not endorsed by the party's state executive when it was revealed the morning after his preselection that he had previously provided a character reference in court for a child sex offender.

Ms Campbell, the Liberal Party and the City of Melbourne have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Nine arrested after teenager bashed and tied to tree
World.content:
Nine people have been arrested and three charged after a 17-year-old boy was bashed and tied to a tree.

A jogger found the teenager in bushland off Cape Pallarenda Road in Townsville about 6:35am on July 18.

Three people have been charged with offences, including torture. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

A 13-year-old Deeragun boy was charged on July 24 with four offences, including torture. He appeared in Townsville Childrens Court on July 24.

A 35-year-old Kirwan woman was charged with five offences, including torture and unlawfully detain/confine on July 28. She remains in custody and will face Townsville Magistrates Court on September 28.

A 14-year-old Kirwan girl was charged with four offences, including torture and assault while in armed company and has been dealt with under the Youth Justice Act.

Another six people were arrested on August 7 and are yet to be charged.

Investigations continue.

World.title: Imam calls out pro-Palestine rally comments as 'inappropriate'
World.content:
A prominent Australian imam has said comments made at a pro-Palestinian rally at which another imam described October 7, 2023 as a "day of pride" and "victory" were inappropriate.

Australian National Imams Council (ANIC) President Sheikh Shadi Asuleiman was on Friday called to give evidence at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, which has this week been examining the drivers of antisemitism and radicalisation in the community.

Born to Palestinian immigrants and raised in Sydney, Sheikh Shadi is also the founder of the United Muslims of Australia, a centre which seeks to engage and support the Muslim community.

He was asked about his response to an incident on October 8, 2023, in which Sheikh Ibrahim Dadoun addressed a pro-Palestinian rally at Lakemba in Sydney's south-west, following terrorist group Hamas's attack on southern Israel.

Sheikh Ibrahim told the crowd he was "smiling" and "happy".

"I'm elated, it's a day of courage, it's a day of pride, it's a day of victory. This is the day we've been waiting for," he said at the time.

'Nothing to celebrate'

Speaker Sheikh Ibrahim Dadoun described the Hamas attacks as an act of resistance. (ABC News)

The rally attracted widespread criticism, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese saying at the time there was "nothing to celebrate" about the attacks in southern Israel.

Sheikh Ibrahim posted a statement to Facebook the day after the rally, stating he did not "express any support" for the loss of lives on either side of the war in his speech.

"I do not condone nor celebrate the killing of innocent people on any side, particularly women and children," he said in the statement.

"In my speech [on October 8, 2023] when I said 'I'm smiling and I'm happy' … I was referring only to the fact of the Palestinian people breaking the blockade after 16 years of grave suffering."

Sheikh Shadi said Sheikh Ibrahim had resigned from his director position at the ANIC some time before the incident, and his comments were made without the knowledge or approval of ANIC.

"We believe the comments that Ibrahim Dadoun made on the 8th of October were inappropriate, especially during a time of heightened tension and a time where communities need to come together," Sheikh Shadi said on Friday.

Sheikh 'very cooperative'

Imam Ibrahim is the former director of ANIC. (ABC News: Cecilia Connell )

Sheikh Shadi said the ANIC sought explanation from Sheikh Ibrahim, who was provided counselling.

"Our approach … at ANIC is to always engage with our members," he said.

"Our philosophy is very strong when it comes to excluding anyone even when they make serious mistakes, [exclusion] is unhelpful for the organisation, for the individual and for the community.

"We do believe that religious leaders have responsibility in their rhetoric and narrative and when we saw cooperation from an individual of concern, then we would like to keep these people in the folds of the Australian National Imams Council."

Sheikh Shadi said the ANIC spoke with Sheikh Ibrahim, who was "very cooperative" and "knew that it was a mistake to use that language".

"We asked him to clarify himself in the public, and he did so," he said.

"We did not see there was a need for further action."

Media coverage criticised

Sheikh Shadi says Sheikh Ibrahim was "very cooperative" when spoken with about the incident. (ABC News)

The commission heard ANIC signed a joint statement with a number of other Muslim organisations which addressed the comments made by Sheikh Ibrahim.

The statement said some media outlets took Sheikh Ibrahim's words "out of context".

"Throughout his entire speech, the Imam makes no reference to innocent lives lost," the statement said.

"We deplore the media coverage and the rhetoric used to incite anti-Palestinian sentiments."

Counsel representing various Jewish communal organisations, Nicholas Bender SC, asked Sheikh Shadi if the statement ANIC supported was "appropriate and adequate" in the way in which it described Sheikh Ibrahim's speech.

Sheikh Shadi said ANIC agreed with the "general sentiment" expressed in the statement, but said the organisation did not play a primary role in drafting the statement.

An 'attack on all communities'

Sheikh Shadi said ANIC agreed with the "general sentiment" expressed in the statement. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Sheikh Shadi said ANIC met with members of the Jewish community in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack on December 14, 2025.

"We stood by them and reiterated many, many times that while this is a targeted attack on the Jewish community, it is an attack on all communities, including the Muslim community," he said.

Sheikh Shadi was also asked to discuss ANIC's role in identifying and addressing ideologically motivated extremism in the community.

"We don't use the term 'radicalisation' within our circles but we do believe that sometimes religious leaders from the Muslim community might have concerning ideologies that need to be addressed," he said.

"The best way we that we do that is through awareness and engagement."

World.title: 'No money left': Man stole $220k in three months to fund online bets
World.content:
A Tasmanian man stole more than $220,000 from his employer in the space of three months to fund his online gambling addiction, telling police "there was no money left".

A court heard Christopher Lee William Ford Brown set up five personal bank accounts to receive the money, transferring it to his online gambling accounts within 20 minutes to "gamble away".

He pleaded guilty to 20 offences, including 15 counts of fraud, and was sentenced in the Supreme Court in Hobart to serve six months in jail, with the rest of the sentence suspended.

Brown was employed as an administration officer at industry advocacy body Salmon Tasmania in early 2024, where his job involved processing supplier payments.

Labor MPs call for tougher gambling reforms The Albanese government faces internal pressure to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more MPs calling for sweeping amendments.

The court heard he created false bank account details and did not provide invoices to Salmon Tasmania's bookkeeper, KPMG.

Instead, the money from 15 transactions made its way into his online gambling accounts with Sportsbet, Neds and Bet365, as well as through in-person gambling at TAB outlets.

Four months after starting the job, he requested a meeting with Salmon Tasmania chief executive officer Luke Martin where he disclosed that he had been stealing money.

Brown was fired, KPMG conducted an audit and the matter was referred to Tasmania Police.

Christopher Lee William Ford Brown had accounts with several online betting companies. (Giulio Saggin: ABC News)

In an interview with police, summarised to the court by Chief Justice Chris Shanahan, Brown had said he was chasing his losses.

"You had always intended to win back and repay what you had taken, but that never eventuated," Chief Justice Shanahan said.

This included opening another bank account called "Sam Tasmania" to deposit winnings in an attempt to repay the organisation.

Insurer AIG indemnified Salmon Tasmania for the loss, and the court ordered Brown to repay AIG.

Gambling 'the primary cause of problems in his life'

The court heard Christopher Lee William Ford Brown had since self-excluded from all forms of online gambling. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

It was the third time Brown had been sentenced for dishonesty offences, all of which occurred to fund his online gambling addiction, the court was told.

He has since self-excluded from all forms of online gambling.

He has been diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which the court heard made him "particularly vulnerable" to online gambling, but that he has been receiving treatment and counselling.

This identified that gambling was "the primary cause of problems in his life".

Sentencing was significantly delayed while the court looked into whether the required medication would be available in Tasmania's prison system.

Chief Justice Shanahan said Brown had numerous earlier opportunities to recognise the severity of his gambling addiction, but had not done so.

He said Brown's decision to self-disclose his offending to his employer was a mitigating factor in sentencing.

"Your offending was serious as it involved a significant sum of money. It was a gross breach of trust. It had elements of opportunism about it," Chief Justice Shanahan told the court.

"It occurred over a short period, however you self-reported your offending."

Brown was sentenced to two years in prison, with 18 months suspended. He will be required to self-exclude from all forms of gambling upon his release.

World.title: Man says he was 'very scared' during alleged Alan Jones bedroom assault
World.content:
A man accusing Alan Jones of historical indecent assault has told a court he followed the broadcaster's alleged direction to have a shower and come out in a robe because he did not want to disappoint Mr Jones.

Complainant J, who alleges Mr Jones indecently assaulted him on nine occasions in 2003 and 2004, has been cross-examined by barrister Gabrielle Bashir about his account of the allegations in the Sydney Local Court trial.

The Crown and Complainant J said he was 17 at the time of the first alleged assault in 2003, but under cross-examination Complainant J agreed he may have been 18.

The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 20 counts of assault with act of indecency and two counts of sexual touching relating to six alleged victims between 2003 and 2020.

The complainant, now in his 40s, alleged Mr Jones asked him to wear "a robe and nothing else" during a visit to his Fitzroy Falls property in 2004.

The date of the trip to Fitzroy Falls is alleged to have happened at some time in 2004, when Complainant J was 18 or 19.

Gabrielle Bashir arrives at court on Friday. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Mr Jones's barristers have pushed Complainant J on why he did not stop the alleged behaviour at any point, and why he followed the alleged instruction to wear a robe when he said Mr Jones had assaulted him several times already that day.

"You must have understood that this was some kind of suggestion of getting ready for sexual activity?" Ms Bashir said. "Yes," Complainant J replied. "You could have put your pants back on," Ms Bashir said. "I could have," Complainant J replied.

Complainant J told the court he "very fearfully" put his robe on but also put on underwear as "protection," and went back out to sit on the lounge with Mr Jones.

Ms Bashir suggested multiple times to Complainant J during cross-examination that he had "concocted" or "fabricated" his story after reading media reports with similar allegations.

'I didn't like when he was disappointed in me'

Complainant J previously said he received weekly payments from the broadcaster to help with his sporting career, and that he was grateful for the money and did not want it to stop.

"[Mr Jones] never said he'd pull the money if you didn't do what he wanted, did he?" Ms Bashir asked.

"No, but I didn't like when he was disappointed in me," Complainant J said.

"It was not a good time, not a good feeling."

Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to all charges. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

The court also heard there were several staff at Fitzroy Farm on the occasion Complainant J visited, but he agreed he did not raise the alarm or tell anyone there about what he alleges Mr Jones had done.

Complainant J was then taken to allegations he made about an assault in the bedroom, where he says Mr Jones hugged him, kissed him and then moved so that their genitals touched as their robes parted.

"You would have pushed him off you if he ever tried to do such a thing, wouldn't you?" Ms Bashir asked. "I didn't," Complainant J replied. "I was very scared. "In that room that was as scared as I've ever been."

The cross-examination has sought to pick apart Complainant J's account of the allegations, and Ms Bashir has suggested there were inconsistencies between his statement to police and the evidence given in court.

Complainant J admitted at times that his memory of the events had changed, but told the court he was doing his best to recall alleged events from more than two decades ago.

Complainant J was also asked whether an earlier comment he made in court referencing Mr Jones's genitals was to "smear" or "humiliate" him.

"You wouldn't know because you've never seen Mr Jones's penis, have you?" Ms Bashir asked. "Yes I have," Complainant J replied.

The complainant was also pushed on why he did not get up and leave when he alleged Mr Jones sat next to him on the bed and asked him to masturbate together.

"I was very scared and thought I had to do that to have it all stop," he said.

He agreed while he was physically strong and an athlete competing in significant competitions at that the time, he was still "young in the head".

Mr Jones's defence team said none of the allegations made by Complainant J ever happened.

World.title: The key takeaways from six days of evidence at NDIS Senate inquiry
World.content:
Not since it was first set up, have the people who rely on and work within the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) faced such significant changes.

The government has proposed a suite of amendments to the laws that govern the scheme, which they say will reduce its cost by more than $30 billion over four years.

Over six days of hearings, senators scrutinised those changes asking how people with disability will be affected, what the impact will be on their families and carers, and what other services will be available to those who lose support.

Labor senator Ellie Whiteaker and Greens senator Jordan Steele-John listen to evidence on the final day of public hearings in the NDIS inquiry. (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

If the changes are made, modelling points to more than 300,000 participants exiting the scheme or being prevented from joining it, so there was not much common ground during the inquiry between what the government wants and the people at the heart of the scheme.

But there was agreement from witnesses across the board that rorting of the system must stop and the scheme's growth must be brought under control so that it can be sustained into the future.

The Senate committee only took submissions for two weeks, but in that time 4,500 groups and individuals wrote in with their concerns.

Among the submissions was a stinging rebuke from state and territory ministers who said the pace of change was too fast, they had not been suitably consulted, and alternative services would not be ready.

There were a number of contentious issues that came up over the hearings. Here's what we heard:

The cut labelled a 'safety issue'

The government has said NDIS funding for participants to engage with their community is a 'runaway' cost that needs to be reined in.

Their plan is to use a provision in the amended legislation that would allow the Commonwealth disability minister of the day to order a percentage cut to any stream of funding they see fit.

Once the legislation passes, the government has said the funding stream used by participants to hire support workers to get out into the community for things like doctors appointments, or to the supermarket, will be cut by 50 per cent.

Participants' budgets for capacity building (which fund therapies) will also be reduced by 10 per cent.

Federal Disability Discrimination Commissioner Rosemary Kayess is worried reduced funding for community participation could isolate participants and put them at risk. (Supplied: AHR)

Disability Discrimination Commissioner Rosemary Kayess said the cuts would mean many participants could find themselves stuck in unsafe environments like those exposed by the Disability Royal Commission.

"They end up in either closed environments or isolated environments, and they are at risk of violence, abuse and exploitation," she said.

A lived-experience witness said cutting his funding would have a profound impact on his life.

"If this government reduces that community and social participation funding any further, I effectively become a prisoner in my own home," Andrew told the hearing.

No one wants fraud in the scheme

One of the government's main motivations for the sweeping changes is stamping out rorts perpetrated by unscrupulous operators who exploit NDIS participants' packages.

Many witnesses told the inquiry they supported measures that would reduce fraud, overcharging, over-servicing and other sharp practices.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) told the hearings the scheme is an attractive target to criminals due to the scale of expenditure.

The most contentious parts of the NDIS bill With thousands of submissions made to the Senate inquiry into the NDIS bill, these were the most contentious of the changes proposed.

The proposed changes to the NDIS Act would give the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) the power it needs to investigate fraud on its own and address some conflicts of interest.

Several witnesses questioned why the bill did not go further.

"Given that the narrative has been fraud is a significant driver of cost, then this legislation doesn't necessarily go close enough to that," Bronwyn Morris Donovan, from Allied Health Professions, said.

Concern for carers

By providing support for people with disability, the NDIS has made it possible for many family members and carers to access assistance to manage their children's conditions or return to work.

The new legislation could change that.

The draft bill says parents should be responsible for providing "substantial care" such as the personal care, transport and behavioural support that "would reasonably be expected of a parent of a child of a similar age".

Skye Kakoschke-Moore, CEO of Children and Young People with Disability Australia, warns of potential for carer burnout. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The chief executive of Children and Young People with Disability Australia, Skye Kakoschke-Moore, said raising children with disability was not the same as raising children without disability.

"Expecting a parent to single-handedly provide the same level of care and support as a team of skilled, qualified, experienced support workers, risks putting that family into further crisis and may lead to increased instances of carer burnout," Ms Kakoschke-Moore said.

The government has said it wants to move children with autism and developmental delay, with mild to moderate support needs, off the NDIS.

The Thriving Kids program, which is due to begin rolling out in just eight weeks, will provide parents of these children with state-based support.

Advocates raised concern about how few of those services are in place yet.

Draft ministerial powers labelled 'dangerous'

Throughout the hearings there was condemnation from advocates for the proposal to give the NDIS minister the power to cut any NDIS funding stream they deem too costly.

George Taleporos has raised concerns about changes to ministerial powers. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Dr George Taleporos, a disability advocate who was instrumental in designing the NDIS, said the provision would create "a terrifying and dangerous power that will cause harm to disabled people".

Ms Kayess said the ministerial powers were very broad and lacked accountability and parliamentary oversight.

Naomi Anderson, from Villa Manta Disability Rights Legal Service, said putting so much power in one person's hands was a problem.

"We don't know who that person will be in future. We don't know what their budget priorities will be. We're basically giving them the PIN number to the bank account," she said.

What's next?

The inquiry will report back on Friday, August 14.

After that, the Senate will vote on the bill.

The Labor-led committee has already issued an interim report, which provides some idea of their thinking.

It said there should be clarification of how the minister is required to consider participants' safety when deciding to cut funding.

How did the NDIS get so expensive? With more changes surrounding the NDIS just announced, here's everything you need to know about the scheme.

It also called for more detail on "critical supports" that the bill says will not be impacted by cuts to particular funding streams.

It also recommended the bill be passed.

The government does not have enough seats in the Senate to pass the bill on its own, so it will need the support of the Coalition or the Greens.

The Greens and senator David Pocock said they did not support the bill passing.

The question everyone now has is what will it mean for the NDIS and the people who rely on it?

World.title: Doctors step up in bid to tackle Qld's 'hidden waiting lists'
World.content:
Queensland's peak medical body has taken matters into its own hands to try and address the ballooning "waiting list to get on the waiting list".

The state government consistently champions a reduction in the surgery waitlist, with just over 60,000 people waiting as of May, slightly down on the same time last year.

But the Australian Medical Association Queensland (AMAQ) noted the number of people waiting to get onto that list had skyrocketed to more than 362,000, up 15 per cent from a year ago.

AMAQ president associate professor Erica Gannon said a new task force will aim to tackle the issue.

Erica Gannon says AMAQ's aim was to work to find "sensible solutions". (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

"We know patients are spending months and sometimes years waiting just to find out what care they need," she said.

"This working group is AMA Queensland's contribution to finding sensible solutions that will support more patients being seen."

The six-member group, comprised of doctors across specialities and Queensland, will be chaired by former AMAQ president Dr Nick Yim.

"As a GP in regional Queensland, I'm acutely aware that local public hospitals are not keeping up with the number of patients being referred to them," he said.

The Queensland government’s performance on elective surgery Queensland's government declared victory on elective surgery wait times, but thousands of patients are waiting longer than recommended.

"We have incredible professionals working across our state, but as our population grows and ages, we are grappling with more complex conditions.

" Seeing hidden waiting lists continue to grow is alarming for patients who deserve timely and appropriate care no matter where they live. "

'Doing everything we can'

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie was asked why it was the responsibility of doctors, rather than the government, to address systemic health issues.

Jarrod Bleijie says the government is doing everything it can to reduce the waiting list. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"The government's doing everything we can to reduce the waiting lists, and we have seen some success in that regard," he said.

"We've been in office for just over a year and a half. I think reasonable people, reasonable Queenslanders, would forgive us for being in office for a year and a half, tackling these big issues, where we are seeing the results coming through."

Shadow treasurer Shannon Fentiman said it was an "embarrassing" indictment on the government and Health Minister Tim Nicholls.

Labor shadow health minister Shannon Fentiman. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"It is unthinkable that the doctors have now seen this extra 70,000 Queenslanders on the waitlist and said 'we need to do something about this'. Where's the health minister?" she said.

"These are the forgotten Queenslanders. They might need life-saving surgery, but they won't know because they simply cannot get in to see a specialist."

Dr Yim highlighted the health system pressure felt in his hometown of Hervey Bay, symptomatic of strain across regional Queensland.

More than 14,000 patients were waiting to see a specialist in May, and almost 60 per cent of the most urgent patients weren't seen within clinically recommended times.

Dr Nick Yim says local public hospitals are not keeping up with the number of patients being referred to them. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi )

"That is almost 5,000 patients in Bundaberg and Hervey Bay in just a two-month period who weren't able to see a specialist close to where they live," he said.

"Sadly, across Queensland, it isn't much better, with 25,539 Cairns patients waiting for an initial appointment and over 45 per cent of Category 1 patients not being seen within the clinically recommended time.

"Central Queensland's wait list has jumped almost 46 per cent compared with last year while the number of initial appointments held has fallen 3.5 per cent, with only 38 per cent of all patients seen within clinically recommended times."

The AMAQ outpatients working group will deliver recommendations to the government in early 2027.

World.title: ‘Chapter of Genesis’: Judge gets biblical over sacked Qantas workers
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Chapter of Genesis’: Judge gets biblical over sacked Qantas workers Chris Zappone August 7, 2026 — 1:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A six-year wait for penalty payments by long-suffering Qantas ground crew who were illegally sacked by the airline is a step closer to ending after a judge referenced Adam and Eve’s original sin to expedite compensation bogged down by lengthy delays. Justice Michael Lee, in Federal Court in Sydney on Thursday, said he will speed up payments for the sacked Qantas workers by decoupling $38 million in penalties from a larger $120 million scheme which will require more time to implement. Justice Michael Lee and former Qantas worker Ryan Perrett. SMH/Supplied The years-long, drawn-out process to determine compensation has frustrated many of the 1820 ground crew affected, leading one former employee – Ryan Perrett – to request Justice Lee remove the administrators, law firm Maurice Blackburn, from the case. Lee, famous for his erudition, told Perrett: “I must say to you frankly, my attitude towards that, Mr Perrett, is that since the third chapter of Genesis we’ve all been subject to the fall and we all make mistakes, and people of goodwill can make mistakes and they frankly admitted a mistake.



“It’s important to recognise that, with the benefit of hindsight, people learn from these things.” The third chapter of Genesis in the Bible tells the story of original sin in the Garden of Eden, where a snake tempts Eve to eat forbidden fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and Eve shares it with Adam. The case has resulted in the former Qantas workers waiting years for compensation; Lee in 2025 ruled that their sacking in 2020 by Qantas, effective in 2021, was illegal. In addition to the $120 million in compensation Qantas agreed to pay, Lee imposed a separate $90 million penalty on the airline, of which $50 million was paid to the Transport Workers’ Union, which brought the case. Delays in processing compensation before the July deadline prompted Maurice Blackburn last week to seek an extension until October. The law firm sought the extension just 10 days before the deadline, a development that infuriated former Qantas employees like Perrett. The legal firm apologised to the court for the delay.



Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared Underscoring the frustration of Qantas’ former employees is the lack of transparency in the compensation process, an issue the judge acknowledged. Many of the former baggage handlers have struggled to find full employment since being sacked. Perrett told the court he hadn’t “received any communication from the TWU since they won the $50 million”, noting the first word they heard from the TWU since Lee’s 2025 ruling awarding the penalty was in July, days before the compensation scheme was scheduled to be completed. Lee said he accepted as “entirely genuine” the apology from Maurice Blackburn for how it informed him of the delays caused by a number of independent medical examinations that didn’t satisfy the requirements of the law firm for deciding compensation. “I can understand workers feeling a sense of great frustration that the Transport Workers’ Union got money quicksticks and yet the workers have not got any money for this lengthy period,” Lee said.



Lawyer for Maurice Blackburn Adam Hochroth SC explained the delay arose after an independent medical examiner employed to evaluate the health of sacked workers produced 111 reports “which the administrator didn’t consider” were at a level required to determine compensation. Another delay was caused by a rule requiring a person compensated after getting treatment under Medicare to reimburse the scheme from their payout. Maurice Blackburn was granted an extension to complete the $120 million compensation scheme. In describing his rationale, Lee again invoked the Book of Genesis: “Unlike Lot’s wife, we must not look back. We are in the situation we’re in. The question is where we go from here. “I explained in my earlier reasons that the reason this matter is still before me was the coupling of the payments of compensation to the payment of the residual of the penalty amount.



Related Article Courts Justice Lee blasted Qantas for 1820 illegal sackings. Now he’s turned on the workers’ lawyers “Thus I’ve explained the rationale for this approach elsewhere [and] I’m satisfied and I need to adopt a different course,” said the judge, suggesting the reality was that any continuing method of penalty payments “tethered to” the compensation scheme will “have embedded in it the scheme’s timetable”. A Maurice Blackburn spokesperson said the court’s orders will allow workers to receive their share of the penalty payment in the coming weeks. “We are continuing to work hard to ensure compensation assessments are completed and that compensation is distributed to workers as soon as possible,” they said. “This case has always been about achieving justice for the workers whose lives were upended by Qantas’ unlawful conduct, and our focus remains firmly on delivering that outcome.” The TWU welcomed the decision. “It is fair and just that workers who spent decades at the airline, many of whom were never able to find other employment following their illegal sacking, would be apportioned a greater amount of the penalty,” national secretary Michael Kaine said.



“It’s now up to Maurice Blackburn to finalise the compensation process as quickly as possible so workers can move on with their lives,” he said. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Craig Bellamy makes huge call on his coaching future
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 Craig Bellamy makes huge call on his coaching future Adrian Proszenko August 7, 2026 — 1:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Craig Bellamy has ended speculation about his future by confirming he will continue as Melbourne coach next year. Bellamy, one of the game’s greatest mentors, has long considered his position on a year-to-year basis. The veteran coach was diagnosed in April with a form of neurodegenerative disorder, further clouding his future. Melbourne coach Craig Bellamy. Getty Images However, he revealed he will continue in the role during a pre-game press-conference on Friday at HBF Park in Perth, where his side is preparing to take on Manly on Saturday. “I’ll be coaching next year, but yeah, I think that that might be the end,” Bellamy told reporters. “But anyway, we’ll see what happens.”



Asked if he was keen to finish up on a brighter note than this year, given his team is likely to miss the play-offs, Bellamy said: “I’d like to, yeah. Like I say, they’re all working hard at the moment, so that’s all we need to do. “And as I said, we still want to try and finish the season on an upward note, you know? So we’ll see what happens. Like I say, as long as we keep preparing well and training well, it gives us a chance to do that.” Bellamy’s decision to stay means star player Cameron Munster will likely do the same. Getty Images Bellamy’s decision is likely to result in Storm star Cameron Munster staying put. Munster, who will make an early return from knee surgery against the Sea Eagles after sustaining a cartilage injury, has publicly stated that if Bellamy continues coaching at the club, so will he. Munster, who is contracted until the end of next year, had been granted early permission to negotiate with the PNG Chiefs. However, the Bellamy development will now likely result in Melbourne retaining the Maroons playmaker.



Bellamy said the pair share a strong bond. “We have, and it’s been a long one, too, you know?” Bellamy said. “We’ve seen ups and downs, ins and outs, and whatever together. World.title: ‘Chapter of Genesis’: Judge gets biblical over sacked Qantas workers
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘Chapter of Genesis’: Judge gets biblical over sacked Qantas workers Chris Zappone August 7, 2026 — 1:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A six-year wait for penalty payments by long-suffering Qantas ground crew who were illegally sacked by the airline is a step closer to ending after a judge referenced Adam and Eve’s original sin to expedite compensation bogged down by lengthy delays. Justice Michael Lee, in Federal Court in Sydney on Thursday, said he will speed up payments for the sacked Qantas workers by decoupling $38 million in penalties from a larger $120 million scheme which will require more time to implement. Justice Michael Lee and former Qantas worker Ryan Perrett. SMH/Supplied The years-long, drawn-out process to determine compensation has frustrated many of the 1820 ground crew affected, leading one former employee – Ryan Perrett – to request Justice Lee remove the administrators, law firm Maurice Blackburn, from the case. Lee, famous for his erudition, told Perrett: “I must say to you frankly, my attitude towards that, Mr Perrett, is that since the third chapter of Genesis we’ve all been subject to the fall and we all make mistakes, and people of goodwill can make mistakes and they frankly admitted a mistake.



“It’s important to recognise that, with the benefit of hindsight, people learn from these things.” The third chapter of Genesis in the Bible tells the story of original sin in the Garden of Eden, where a snake tempts Eve to eat forbidden fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and Eve shares it with Adam. The case has resulted in the former Qantas workers waiting years for compensation; Lee in 2025 ruled that their sacking in 2020 by Qantas, effective in 2021, was illegal. In addition to the $120 million in compensation Qantas agreed to pay, Lee imposed a separate $90 million penalty on the airline, of which $50 million was paid to the Transport Workers’ Union, which brought the case. Delays in processing compensation before the July deadline prompted Maurice Blackburn last week to seek an extension until October. The law firm sought the extension just 10 days before the deadline, a development that infuriated former Qantas employees like Perrett. The legal firm apologised to the court for the delay.



Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared Underscoring the frustration of Qantas’ former employees is the lack of transparency in the compensation process, an issue the judge acknowledged. Many of the former baggage handlers have struggled to find full employment since being sacked. Perrett told the court he hadn’t “received any communication from the TWU since they won the $50 million”, noting the first word they heard from the TWU since Lee’s 2025 ruling awarding the penalty was in July, days before the compensation scheme was scheduled to be completed. Lee said he accepted as “entirely genuine” the apology from Maurice Blackburn for how it informed him of the delays caused by a number of independent medical examinations that didn’t satisfy the requirements of the law firm for deciding compensation. “I can understand workers feeling a sense of great frustration that the Transport Workers’ Union got money quicksticks and yet the workers have not got any money for this lengthy period,” Lee said.



Lawyer for Maurice Blackburn Adam Hochroth SC explained the delay arose after an independent medical examiner employed to evaluate the health of sacked workers produced 111 reports “which the administrator didn’t consider” were at a level required to determine compensation. Another delay was caused by a rule requiring a person compensated after getting treatment under Medicare to reimburse the scheme from their payout. Maurice Blackburn was granted an extension to complete the $120 million compensation scheme. In describing his rationale, Lee again invoked the Book of Genesis: “Unlike Lot’s wife, we must not look back. We are in the situation we’re in. The question is where we go from here. “I explained in my earlier reasons that the reason this matter is still before me was the coupling of the payments of compensation to the payment of the residual of the penalty amount.



Related Article Courts Justice Lee blasted Qantas for 1820 illegal sackings. Now he’s turned on the workers’ lawyers “Thus I’ve explained the rationale for this approach elsewhere [and] I’m satisfied and I need to adopt a different course,” said the judge, suggesting the reality was that any continuing method of penalty payments “tethered to” the compensation scheme will “have embedded in it the scheme’s timetable”. A Maurice Blackburn spokesperson said the court’s orders will allow workers to receive their share of the penalty payment in the coming weeks. “We are continuing to work hard to ensure compensation assessments are completed and that compensation is distributed to workers as soon as possible,” they said. “This case has always been about achieving justice for the workers whose lives were upended by Qantas’ unlawful conduct, and our focus remains firmly on delivering that outcome.” The TWU welcomed the decision. “It is fair and just that workers who spent decades at the airline, many of whom were never able to find other employment following their illegal sacking, would be apportioned a greater amount of the penalty,” national secretary Michael Kaine said.



“It’s now up to Maurice Blackburn to finalise the compensation process as quickly as possible so workers can move on with their lives,” he said. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Winston Peters says Pacific missed chance to issue statement after Chinese missile test
World.content:
Foreign Minister Winston Peters says the Pacific missed an opportunity not to issue a joint statement soon after China launched a nuclear-capable missile into waters near Tuvalu.

It's unclear whether a consensus will be reached at today's Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Foreign Ministers' Meeting, with Peters labelling it a "delicate issue".

Peters is in Fiji for the meeting along with counterparts from 17 other Pacific countries, in preparation for the leaders' meeting in Palau, in early September.

It's been a month since China test-launched a nuclear-capable ballistic missile with a dummy warhead into the Pacific Ocean - a nuclear free zone.

It was met with condemnation from some Pacific leaders, and Christopher Luxon said the New Zealand government made clear to China that the move was unacceptable - but there has not been a unanimous statement from Pacific nations.

Peters said New Zealand had been pushing for one.

"It's a very delicate issue," he said, suggesting some countries would come to the meeting with their minds made up.

"The roadblock is that if you've had a predetermined position, any discussion here and any logic and reasoning will not land," he said.

"We'll see whether logic prevails in this debate, or whether the debate has already been settled by people having a predetermined position from which they will not move."

The PIF Foreign Leaders' Meeting group photo in Fiji on 7 August 2026. RNZ / Lauren Crimp

Peters would not name the countries he believed were holding things back.

He said it was not too late to take a joint position however it should have been done sooner: "the sooner the better."

The countries should not be in a position where they could not reach consensus on the matter, said Peters.

"At this point in time, we've got one third of the world's surface, there's a desperation for serious funds when it comes to resilience building in this part of the world," he said.

"The economic situation is not good, so we need each other more than ever, and we need international recognition as well more than ever."

Peters had a brief discussion with Australia's foreign minister Penny Wong on Friday morning ahead of the meeting, but would not say whether the two countries were on the same page.

He said there would also be discussion about how partner countries work with PIF following the controversial decision to ban them - including heavy hitters like China and the US - from last year's meeting in the Solomon Islands.

Peters has spoken out repeatedly about "outsiders" influencing the Solomon Islands Prime Minister Jeremiah Manele to implement the ban, which Manele denied, arguing the block made sense while PIF leaders considered how best to respond to the increasing interest from partners wanting a seat at the regional decision-making table.

"We need their help," Peters said.

"This idea of tiering people and all sorts of this part of the discussion, if it means that you actually lose the chance for buy-in by serious countries, then that'll be a big mistake."

Fiji's foreign minister Sakiasi Ditoka opened the meeting with a call for unity.

"Even as our strategic environment becomes more complex, the Pacific response should not be fragmentation or division," he said, as the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Minister's meeting kicked off.

"It should be greater regional solidarity, stronger consensus and continued confidence in our own regional institutions and processes."

He said the foreign ministers had a "unique responsibility," helping to shape how the Pacific "engages the world, manages these partnerships, and protects the integrity of our regional institutions".

Ditoka said the matters before the forum reflect that responsibility, from "strengthening our peace and security architecture", to advancing the 2050 "international engagement strategy" and "deepening regional integration".

He also stated it was about "ensuring our partnerships continue to serve Pacific priorities".

"Together they represent practical steps towards implementing the vision set out in the 2050 strategy for the blue Pacific continent."

The secretary general Baron Waqa followed, saying guidance from the foreign ministers would continue to shape the evolution of regionalism and the "trajectory of regional institutions".

For his part, he said, "allow me to reaffirm that the secretariat remains committed to supporting a forum that is increasingly strategic" and responsible.

World.title: Bad week? Try being a Chris
World.content:
Analysis: It's been a rough week in politics and if it's not one Chris having a bad day, it's the other.

That was the case on Friday when four shocker days for the prime minister swung to the left following a woeful poll result for Labour's Chris Hipkins.

Christopher Luxon's foot-in-mouth moments would have been enough on their own without adding in his foreign minister telling a Chinese-Kiwi Parliamentary colleague to "go back to where you've come from", and unemployment at an 11-year high, with just 92 days until the election.

A sympathetic observer would look to Luxon's time at the helm and say he's had bad luck with being handed a complicated coalition, an economy on its knees, and an unpredictable US president.

Yet, Luxon is the first to ignore the complexities of Covid - a worldwide pandemic never seen in our time - and the problems that created for Labour and Jacinda Ardern.

So, on that basis his starting point for all prime ministers is that regardless of the crisis - health or economic or both - it's not an excuse for the government of the day's performance, or lack thereof.

That's a problematic baseline for a governing party that sold itself as the economic fixer.

While there are plenty of improvements to be celebrated - turning points in some (not all) business confidence, inflation at times getting closer to the target bracket - there are also some nightmare numbers Luxon cannot ignore.

Christopher Luxon. Pool/AFP/Michael Bradley

The biggest one came this week in the form of an unemployment rise to an 11-year high of 5.6 percent.

There are now 171,000 people unemployed and around 8000 more people are experiencing long term unemployment - those out of work for a year or more - this June quarter than in the same quarter last year.

Couple that with Luxon's brainfart moment last weekend where he decided to attack provincial New Zealand small and medium sized businesses (SMEs) telling them they had a "parent-child mentality" and needed to be more "adult" and the prime minister's grip on the economy doesn't look so tight.

Former National Party leader turned Auckland Business Chamber chief executive Simon Bridges summed it up best in a NZ Herald column on Friday morning.

"And to state what I hope is blindingly obvious, but clearly isn't, SMEs are very different from a business with thousands of employees and hundreds of millions or billions in turnover. They didn't, as the Prime Minister says he did, "sit in Illinois for six years" as an executive of consumer goods company Unilever, and they don't think that much about "commercially superior returns, great customer experience and awesome internal culture". Not explicitly anyway. The owner very often is the internal culture, the HR manager, accounts, marketing and everything else, rolled into one. They are busy just surviving. They do their best every day without huge analysis or much if any support.

"Yet, such lowly businesspeople do worry about what the Government does, because the Government in this small nation controls so much in terms of spending, sentiment, policies and programmes. Its taxes, costs and red tape make all the difference, as do its statements and initiatives," Bridges wrote.

It's a scathing reality check for the prime minister who prides himself on getting out of the Wellington bubble and connecting with everyday Kiwis living in the region to find himself managing to offend, and later having to apologise to, what was considered a friendly business audience.

NZ First leader Winston Peters and Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan. RNZ

Supporters have commended Luxon for acknowledging he got it wrong and saying sorry, but there are others who have asked how he stuffed it up in the first place.

The point Luxon was trying to make about him wanting government to get out of the way so that business can thrive is valid, but despite making this point on so many occasions in the past two-and-a-half years to various business audiences he still hasn't nailed the delivery of it.

The other notable gaffe this week was turning a day of celebration in Auckland that the long-awaited CRL finally had an opening date into a confused mess about whether National was going to hold a referendum on MMP.

It was an own goal when instead of concentrating on an infrastructure success, or taking a whack at Labour's plan to ditch National's much-loved Investment Boost policy, Luxon loose-lipped his way into an election promise that even his caucus doubted was real.

National would have breathed a deep sigh of relief when the Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll landed on Friday with some good news for the party.

Not only was it up on 31 percent and ahead of Labour, but the coalition was also in a position to form a government and Luxon was up in the preferred prime minister numbers.

Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Labour has plummeted to 27.8 percent - a dire result that on first glance looks to have come from Luxon ruling out working with Opportunity after the election.

Opportunity has soared to 6 percent in the poll at the expense of Labour.

Labour has been operating on a small-target strategy with policy announcements this election year after learning the lesson of flooding voters in 2023, and losing sight of what the party stood for and was trying to sell.

But the new approach appears to be having its own problems with National getting centrist policy like solar panel loans for households and KiwiSaver policy out ahead of Labour, and leaving the Opposition unable to criticise something it broadly agrees with.

Hipkins also has his own popularity issues to deal with. He's a known quantity having been prime minister before, which he was handed and then had ripped off him when voters went to the polls and chose the other Chris.

He has a difficult job explaining to voters why he'd do a better job second time round.
